Annual Report and Notice of 11th Annual General Meeting for the 
Financial Year 2025-26 to be held through Video Conferencing 
(VC)/Other Audio-Visual Means (OAVM) 
 
Dear Sir/Madam, 
 
This is to inform that the 11th Annual General Meeting (“AGM”) of ACME Solar Holdings 
Limited ("Company") is scheduled to be held on Tuesday, September 29, 2026 at 
03:00 P.M. (IST) through Video Conferencing (VC)/Other Audio Visual Means (OAVM) 
in compliance with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 ("the Act"), 
and SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 ("SEBI 
Listing Regulations") read with applicable circulars thereunder.  
 
Pursuant to Regulations 30 and 34 of the SEBI Listing Regulations, we are submitting 
herewith the Annual Report, which includes inter-alia the Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Report, and Notice convening the 11th AGM (including e-voting 
instructions) (“AGM Notice”) for the financial year 2025-26, which is sent through 
electronic mode to the members of the Company whose names appear in the register 
of members/list of beneficial owners of  depositories and whose  e-mail address are 
registered with the respective depository participant(s) as of Friday, August 28, 
2026. 
 
In compliance with Regulation 36(1)(b) of the SEBI Listing Regulations, physical 
letters providing the weblink along with the exact path to access the Annual Report 
for the financial year 2025-26 and the AGM Notice are dispatched to members, whose 
email addresses are not registered with their respective depository participant(s).  
 
The Company has appointed National Securities Depository Limited (“NSDL”) as the 
e-voting agency. Members of the Company, holding shares in demat form as on 
Wednesday, September 23, 2026, being the cut-off date, will be eligible to cast their 
vote, on all resolutions as set out in the AGM Notice by electronic means, through 
remote e-voting facility which shall commence on Saturday, September 26, 2026, 
from 9:00 A.M. (IST) and end on Monday, September 28, 2026, at 5:00 P.M. (IST), 
or through e-voting (Insta Poll) at the AGM.

Reliability & Responsiveness, 
Reimagined
India’s strides toward the Viksit Bharat vision for 2047 stand at a defining crossroads 
where growth, sustainability and energy security are no longer separate journeys 
but a single, shared path forward. As our nation accelerates renewable energy 
adoption, the transition cannot realise its full potential without progressively 
replacing hydrocarbons across the economy. Today, hydrocarbons account for a 
large share of energy consumption in multiple forms — including fuels, fertilisers 
and chemicals — presenting a significant opportunity to build a broader and more 
integrated roadmap for renewable energy growth.
As electrification expands into sectors that have traditionally relied on the flexibility 
and responsiveness of hydrocarbons, the energy system must offer comparable 
reliability, agility and responsiveness. This will require a renewable energy-led grid 
that is supported by storage, flexible generation and intelligent grid infrastructure.
Powering India’s ambition demands more than megawatts on paper; it calls 
for energy that arrives precisely when the grid calls for it, reliable in delivery and 
matched to an economy accelerating in every direction. The conversation around 
renewable energy is evolving too, moving beyond how much clean power is 
generated to how dependably it is delivered, day and night, season after season.
ACME Solar sees this shift as an invitation to lead. In FY 2026, we deepened our 
commitment to reliability by scaling our BESS* and FDRE** portfolios, weaving 
storage and flexibility into the very architecture of renewable power so that clean 
energy becomes not just abundant but unfailingly present when the moment 
demands it. We are working closely with the grid to develop solutions that can 
reliably meet short-duration and time-sensitive power demand.
With India’s Net Zero pledge by 2070 as the horizon, the path ahead calls for 
solutions that combine scale with steadfastness and vision with delivery. 
ACME Solar is architecting that future today, reimagining renewable energy not 
merely as a greener alternative but as a dependable force, one capable of 
strengthening the grid, powering ambition and steering India confidently towards 
a low-carbon tomorrow.

ACME Solar Holdings Limited | Annual Report 2025-26

Dear Shareholders,
It gives me great pleasure to write 
to you about a year of impressive 
business performance even amid 
economic disruptions triggered by 
geopolitical uncertainties.
We are at a critical juncture 
as global transition towards 
renewable energy is gaining 
fresh momentum amid growing 
geopolitical uncertainties and 
disruptions to the global oil 
trade particularly due to West 
Asia conflict. To reduce our 
exposure to external energy 
shocks and strengthen energy 
security, we need to accelerate 
the electrification of sectors 
currently dependent on 
crude oil and further scale up 
investments in sustainable and 
renewable energy.
In sync with the surge in global 
green power capacity, energy 
storage has gained significance. 
When paired with battery and 
right power electronics systems, 
renewables energy can provide 
responsive energy, grid inertia and 
long steady electricity at rates 
cheaper than fossil fuels, even 
when the sun doesn’t shine or the 
wind doesn’t blow.
Ranked among India’s leading 
renewable energy Independent 
Power Producers (IPPs), ACME Solar 
contributes significantly to the 
nation’s transition to renewables. 
Our steady rise in the clean 
energy landscape prompted us to 
focus on battery energy storage 
systems (BESS) to power the next 
phase of growth.
Aligned to India’s Green 
Mission
The rapid stride in renewable power 
reflects a steady progress towards 
the self-reliant, cost-effective 
energy for our people which are 
still underserved. As the country 
strides toward its Viksit Bharat vision 
for 2047, our per capita energy 
consumption needs to move from 
current ~1,500 kWh by 3x. This should 
itself be an audacious goal for all 
of us in the industry to create our 
roadmap for profitable growth.
Our goal to reach 500 GW by 2030 
itself demonstrates that India can 
think big and can charter a path 
to scale up to unprecedent levels. 
We believe that capacity created 
in the industry in the last decade 
would be very helpful for moving 
towards the Viksit Bharat target.
The evolving dynamics have 
pushed renewable power 
companies to stare at a 
transformative journey, aided by 
clear goals, agile supply chains, 
supportive policies.
Driven by the triple imperatives of 
energy security, affordability, and 
sustainability, the government 
plans structural policy reforms to 
align public financial flows with its 
clean energy goals.
At ACME Solar, we are committed 
to seizing the opportunity by 
innovating business process, plant 
configuration and technology 
adoption. We work with grid 
operations, regulatory system 
and on policy advocacy level 
with government to ensure that 
some of the infrastructure lags 
in availability do not affect the 
capacity addition and financial 
return. We will be very nimble 
working with all stakeholders 
to create market, solution and 
regulatory framework so that 
most effective solution is delivered 
to the customers.
As this opportunity unfolds on 
India’s booming green power turf, 
we set out for a big leap, backed 
by our 20 years of experience in 
energy management.
As a listed clean energy producer 
with a portfolio of FDRE, BESS, 
solar, hybrid and wind projects, 
we develop, build, own, operate 
and maintain utility-scale 
renewable energy projects 
through our in-house engineering, 
procurement and construction 
(EPC) division and operation 
and maintenance (O&M) team, 
and generate stable, long-term 
revenue through fixed-tariff 
power purchase agreements 
(PPAs) largely with central and 
state government-backed 
entities. We will always look for 
experimenting new technologies, 
new configurations, new business 
solutions and new customer base 
to broaden our offerings at scale 
and financial prudence.
Our renewable energy generation 
contracted capacity scaled 
8,070 MW1 by the end of FY 2026, 
comprising an operational 
project capacity of 2,982 MW2, 
under-construction contracted 
capacity of 5,088 MW3, PPA signed 
project capacity of 3,288 MW4, 
and under-construction LOA 
project capacity of 1,800 MW5.
Storage, the New Frontier
After capacity, the next major 
step for renewable energy 
generators is storage. As batteries 
proliferate, power companies 
use them in novel ways, such 
as handling big swings in 
electricity generation from 
solar and wind farms, reducing 
congestion on transmission lines, 
voltage fluctuations, frequency 
fluctuations, grid unbalancing 
and preventing blackouts 
and brownouts.

The year under review marks the 
beginning of our journey into 
BESS that serves as the base 
for our firm and dispatchable 
renewable energy (FDRE) projects. 
As India rapidly tenders 
renewable energy and storage 
capacities, the Central Electricity 
Authority estimates that 411.4 GWh 
energy storage will be needed 
by 2031-32.6 As developers 
commission all their solar and 
FDRE projects pipeline, it will create 
more duck curve situation in the 
grid which will push the evening 
and morning peak along with time 
shift in the night. All this shows 
that we may be conservative in 
estimating energy storage needs 
for next five years.
During FY 2026, we operationalised 
1.3 GWh of BESS capacity in 
Rajasthan, taking our total 
operational BESS portfolio to 
3.6 GWh7. This marks a significant 
milestone in our storage journey 
and reinforces our position as an 
early mover in utility-scale BESS 
deployment in India. The duck 
curve created due to scaled 
operationalisation of renewable 
capacity in the industry is creating 
a significant arbitrage opportunity 
for BESS operations, as electricity 
prices decline during mid-day 
hours and spike up during the 
evening peak. This enables us to 
procure power from the market 
at lower tariffs during the day 
and sell it at higher prices during 
peak non-solar hours through our 
BESS operations.
We have also made significant 
progress in securing grid 
connectivity for our storage 
portfolio. We have secured over 
10 GWh of BESS connectivity, with 
a further 11 GWh of connectivity 
applications submitted under 
the CERC right-of-first-refusal 
(ROFR) framework currently under 
approval.7 Our development 
strategy is focused on leveraging 
available connectivity to 
commission battery-linked, 
night-time capacity ahead of the 
corresponding commissioning 
of FDRE projects as per 
GNA timelines.
This approach enables us to 
phase capital deployment 
more efficiently, front-loading 
investments that can be 
commissioned and generate 
revenue earlier, while aligning 
subsequent solar investments 
with grid readiness. It also 
provides greater flexibility in 
managing potential connectivity 
delays and reduces the impact 
of such delays on overall project 
timelines and cash generation.
Storage-based power has 
consequently become a 
significant component of our 
portfolio, reflecting our transition 
beyond a pure-play solar model. 
The increasing integration of 
BESS strengthens our ability to 
provide reliable and dispatchable 
renewable power, while 
enhancing portfolio flexibility, 
optimising capital deployment 
and positioning us to address 
the evolving requirements of 
India’s power grid.
Strengthening Capital For 
Sustainable Growth
During the year, we took a 
significant step forward in 
our capital markets journey 
by successfully completing 
our maiden equity capital 
raise since listing in 2024 - a 
Qualified Institutions Placement 
of INR 28,000 million. The strong, 
diversified participation from both 
existing and new investors in this 
issue reflects the confidence the 
market places in our execution 
track record and growth 
trajectory. The proceeds will help 
us strengthen our balance sheet 
and reduce leverage, positioning 
the Company well for its next 
phase of growth - particularly in 
battery storage, where we are 
advancing the commissioning of 
the BESS component of our FDRE 
projects. This will help mitigate 
risks arising from transmission 
connectivity delays while 
generating additional cashflows 
in the interim period.
Sustainability Powered by 
People
We believe that for any action to 
succeed, it should have people 
in the focus, at the core, and as 
the purpose.
Our resilience, creativity and 
excellence gave us not just a 
solid ground to stand out but 
also instilled within us the ability 
to adapt to a fast- evolving 
landscape and deliver 
beyond expectations.
At ACME Solar, we value 
meritocracy, inclusivity, and 
sustained development. 
We are firmly committed 
to the highest standards 
of corporate governance. 
Our operational frameworks 
stress on transparency, 
accountability and adherence  
to global-best practices.
As a clean energy generator, 
it is redundant to write on our 
climate consciousness. For us, 
sustainability goes beyond the 
mere environmental metrics. 
Sustainability is about creating 
shared prosperity — going 
beyond the ACME family to 
people living in the vicinity of our 
plants and offices. We provide

A Beckoning Future
In a technologically advanced 
and industrious world, energy 
is both the core problem and 
the key solution. While burning 
of fossil fuel gives us the energy 
to run an accelerating world 
order, their emissions threaten 
the very existence of life by 
deepening pollution.
Fossil fuels account for nearly 
3/4th of power generation, but the 
clean energy future is arriving 
fast. As the planet registers 
the highest temperatures on 
record, rising in some places to 
levels incompatible with human 
life, governments around the 
world are pouring trillions of 
dollars into clean energy to cut 
carbon pollution.
These investments are driving 
explosive growth. India, a major 
player in the clean power arena, 
raised its budgetary allocation 
by 32% for FY 2027 to INR 300,000+ 
million for solar energy schemes 
and projects.8 There was a hike in 
outlay for all government policies 
and incentive schemes such as 
PM Surya Ghar Yojana, PM-KUSUM, 
Green Energy Corridors, and 
BESS as the country transitions 
to renewables.
As a significant force in India’s 
green power mission, ACME Solar 
targets 10 GW of operational 
renewable energy capacity by 
2030. We are also participating in 
tenders and winning projects in 
line with our long-term guidance. 
We won 1.4 GW of projects during 
the year under review.
At ACME Solar, we are not merely 
participating in this energy 
transition — we are driving 
the shift through innovation, 
responsibility and purpose. 
We pledge to power progress, 
transform industries and bring 
in a sustainable tomorrow for 
generations to come.
Thank you for your continued trust 
and support.
Regards,
Manoj Kumar Upadhyay

One of the top 10 clean energy 
producers in India finds 
opportunities unfolding even in 
a state of unstable political and 
economic conditions across 
the world and makes strategic 
moves to gain from the country’s 
increasing reliance on renewable 
power sources. What gives ACME 
Solar the robust foundation to set 
an ambitious target in capacity 
building? How did the Company 
perform in a world of rapidly 
evolving business landscape? 
How the company expands its 
horizon to power the next phase of 
growth? Nikhil Dhingra, the Chief 
Executive Officer and a Whole-
Time Director of ACME Solar, 
explains the Company's strategic 
gameplan for the journey ahead. 
Do you think there’s a wave 
of transformation sweeping 
through the world?
Indeed. It is an age of sweeping 
changes across industries 
all over the world. The most 
significant impetus has been 
a major surge in technological 
advancements and their swift and 
expansive growth.
AI, for instance, has redefined 
the way businesses are done 
and emerged as a major 
enabler over the last couple of 
years. Technologies designed to 
resolve climate crisis like global 
warming, environmental pollution, 
greenhouse gas emissions, and 
so on too have found large-scale 
adoption by industries in the face 
of stricter regulatory guidelines.
With AI fuelling unprecedented 
demand for data centres, 
renewables offer a powerful 
pathway to meet this need while 
adhering to green regulations.
The result is the rise of the 
renewable energy sector into 
a USD 2.3-trillion1 industry, 
unleashing huge opportunities 
for clean energy players like 
ACME Solar.
Our approach to this opportunity 
is two-fold. First, we aim to capture 
C&I demand through bespoke 
solutions and commercial 
partnerships with operators. 
Second, we intend to benefit 
indirectly from the broader 
growth in round-the-clock power 
demand flowing through the 
government and utility channels 
we already serve.
As states seek firm, reliable 
power, they will increasingly 
need to procure renewable, 
round-the-clock power that 
is both cost-competitive and 
attractive to all stakeholders. 
This is creating a clear need for 
the right power product: multi-
source RTC solutions that provide 
reliable, firm output rather than 
simply following individual 
generation profiles.
This shift plays directly to the 
strengths of developers like us - 
those with the ability to deliver 
multi-source power, secured 
land and grid connectivity, 
and the capabilities to execute 
complex renewable projects at 
scale. We believe this represents 
a strong and natural fit with our 
core capabilities and positions 
us well to participate in this 
emerging opportunity.
Where do you see India in this 
paradigm shift? Also, where 
does ACME Solar stand in this 
evolving landscape? 
India sits at the fulcrum of an 
industry rebalancing itself rapidly, 
with non-fossil-fuel sources 
making up more than half of 
the country’s total installed 
capacity. This is in line with the 
government’s aggressive target 
of setting up 500 GW of clean 
energy capacity by 2030 as part 
of its pledged Net Zero status by 
2070. The corresponding storage 
capacity projections are in the 
range of 300 GWh by 2030. These 
are attractive numbers for us as a 
leading player in this space, and 
they frame a large addressable 
market for firm renewable and 
storage‑backed solutions.
We are entering a highly 
favourable phase over the next 
few years, with a significant 
opportunity to capture emerging 
demand. Importantly, our 
forward plan is to build 10 GW of 
operational capacity by 2030 
and is already well advanced, 
supported by PPAs, contracted 
capacity and signed capacity. 
We currently have approximately 
3.9 GW2 of projects under signed 
PPAs, which provides a strong 
base of committed demand to be 
serviced over the coming years.
On the demand side, several 
levers will support the build‑up 
to 500 GW by 2030. Key demand 
centres include EV charging, 
industrial electrification and 
various government segments 
that are actively shifting

have connectivity. By developing 
multi-location projects, we can 
bring the night-time component 
online independently, while 
timing the deployment of solar 
capacity to coincide with the 
commissioning of new daytime 
grid connections.

phasing. In the near term, we 
are prioritising battery-linked, 
night-time infrastructure, 
while sequencing solar capex 
to align with expected grid 
connectivity timelines. This allows 
us to front-load investments 
that can generate power and 
revenue, while ensuring daytime 
investments are synchronised 
with grid availability.
Connectivity delays do occur, 
but the regulatory framework 
for government-contracted 
power provides for extensions 
where delays are beyond the 
developer’s control. This protects 
us from penalties when we are 
ready to commission but grid 
connectivity is delayed, allowing 
us to align commissioning with 
the revised timelines.
Importantly, BESS operations is 
already a significant component 
of our portfolio, as we have 
moved away from pure-play 
solar. This materially reduces our 
exposure to GNA connectivity 
delays and allows us to bring 
the night-time component 
online earlier, supporting project 
operations and cash generation 
while GNA catches up.

Market Context
India has crossed 500 GW of installed power generation capacity, with 
renewable energy accounting for approximately 275 GW (52%) of the total 
installed capacity as of March 2026. Renewable sources contributed around 
25% of total electricity generation during FY 2026, supported by continued 
additions in solar and wind capacity. Backed by the Government's target 
of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, the sector is witnessing 
sustained investment across renewable generation, storage and 
transmission infrastructure.
The power market is simultaneously witnessing widening intraday tariff 
differentials. While abundant daytime renewable generation can reduce 
tariffs to as low as INR 0.05 per unit, peak and night-time demand can 
command tariffs of up to INR 10 per unit, significantly strengthening the 
commercial case for storage-backed renewable solutions. At the same 
time, transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity remain critical 
enablers, with limited connectivity availability expected until FY 2028–FY 2029, 
influencing project execution timelines and pipeline conversion.

storage deployment and accelerating industry adoption.

parallel, procurement models are evolving from standalone renewable 
projects towards integrated renewable and storage solutions, requiring 
larger upfront investments, longer development cycles and stronger 
balance sheets. Developers with integrated project development, 
EPC and O&M capabilities, diversified funding sources and disciplined

Global Economy Overview
In CY 2025, the global economy navigated deep 
structural transformations, heavily driven by an 
intensifying technology investment cycle alongside 
evolving macroeconomic shifts. While persistent trade 
fragmentation and heightened geopolitical tensions 
in certain regions restricted broad-based momentum, 
a sharp surge in artificial intelligence infrastructure 
and tech manufacturing provided a crucial stabilising 
force for global economic activity. Propelled by this 
dual dynamic, global GDP growth reached 3.5% in 
CY 2025. Concurrently, widespread monetary policy 
tightening achieved visible success, pulling global 
headline inflation down to 4.1% in CY 2025 as major 
supply chains steadily regain balance.1
Outlook
Looking ahead, the global economic outlook presents 
a cautiously stable but realigned trajectory. Following 
an average growth of 3.5% across the preceding 
period, global GDP growth is projected to moderate 
slightly to 3.0% in CY 2026, with a subsequent 
expansion to 3.4% in CY 2027. Geopolitical conflicts 
and intensifying trade friction continue to act as 
primary catalysts for macro-level uncertainty. 
Concurrently, the global disinflation trend faces a 
temporary pause; headline inflation is expected to 
tick up modestly to 4.7% in CY 2026 before resuming 
its downward path to 3.9% in CY 2027.2 According to 
the IMF, restoring price stability remains complex due 
to persistent services sector inflation, the inflationary 
pressure of newly implemented tariffs, and divergent 
interest rate cycles across major economies.
Against this backdrop, monetary authorities 
must delicately balance price stability objectives 
against growth protection mandates. Fiscal policy 
is shifting towards rebuilding eroded buffers, with 
public capital prioritising critical infrastructure, 
decarbonisation, and social safety nets to anchor 
resilience. Concurrently, developing economies 
navigate restrictive financing conditions and 
unpredictable capital swings driven by shifting 
investor risk tolerances. On the structural front, 
intensified tech-cycle momentum, particularly in 
artificial intelligence infrastructure and advanced 
automation, provides vital channels for efficiency 
optimisation, mitigating underlying structural 
drags. Ultimately, although expansion rates soften, 
a combination of agile policymaking and targeted, 
innovation-led expenditure is anticipated to steer 
the global economy towards a more durable, 
medium-term equilibrium.

As India fast-tracks its journey towards a sustainable

nuclear facilities, the country’s absolute non-fossil 
capacity reached 283 GW.20

50 GW of clean energy annually, India has 
sustained rapid procurement velocity through 
highly successful complex firm and dispatchable 
renewable tenders. India’s progress in the clean 
energy space is reflected in its global standing, now 
ranking firmly as the third-largest renewable energy 
market worldwide.21

According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) 
National Electricity Plan, the storage requirement of 
the grid is estimated to be 411.4 GWh (comprising 
73.93 GW of capacity) by 2032. Battery Energy

bulk of this flexibility, contributing 236 GWh (47.24 GW), 
while the remaining 175 GWh (26.69 GW) will be met 
by Pumped Storage Projects (PSP).26
The commercial feasibility of these massive 
installations has drastically improved as  
global battery pack prices plummeted by 27%  
year-on-year down to a record low benchmark 
of USD 78/MWh* for 4-hour systems. Proactive 
government frameworks actively accelerate 
this pipeline, including the Ministry of Power’s 
mandatory Energy Storage Obligations (ESO) for 
DISCOMs, alongside strict directives forcing future 
utility solar contracts to incorporate co-located 
storage capacity.
While sub-economic pricing and financial closures 
for ultra-low bids create near-term execution 
adjustments, the infrastructure footprint is scaling 
remarkably. The country’s absolute operational 
grid-scale BESS capacity experienced a massive 
surge, climbing from 0.78 GWh at the close of 2025 
to 8.5 GWh by mid-2026.27
Simultaneously, India is capitalising on its immense 
Pumped Hydro Storage (PHS) potential, which 
stands at 181 GW across both on-river and off-river 
configurations. With active construction scaling 
rapidly, the CEA projects operational PHS capacity to 
expand from the baseline to 26.69 GW by 2032. This 
progress is powered by an increasing emphasis on a 
robust energy mix, rising private sector participation, 
and regulatory clarifications establishing storage as 
a distinct, tradable grid asset.

Wind Solar Hybrid and Firm and Dispatchable RE
To address grid intermittency and accelerate 
clean energy integration, India’s power sector is 
undergoing a structural transition driven by the 
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and 
implementing agencies like SECI and SJVN. During 
FY 2025–26, bidding activity shifted decisively away 
from standalone solar toward complex multi-
technology tenders, including Wind-Solar Hybrid 
(WSH), Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy 
(FDRE), and Round-the-Clock (RTC) configurations 
backed by Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). 
While conventional solar and wind offer variable 
outputs, hybrid systems leverage complementary 
diurnal cycles to achieve Capacity Utilisation 
Factors (CUFs). FDRE and RTC projects advance this 
by combining storage with calculated capacity 
overbuild, providing power system reliability 
comparable to conventional thermal plants.
Consequently, FDRE tenders emerged as a 
cost-effective, rapidly deployable alternative to 
new coal-fired assets. Conventional thermal power 
plants demand substantial capital investments, 
carry volatile fuel risks, face execution delays, and 
yield long-term tariffs averaging INR 4–INR 5/kWh.31 
In contrast, FDRE projects feature accelerated 
execution windows and fixed long-term pricing, 
offering a stable and scalable framework to meet 
India’s expanding peak power demand.

Declining Tariffs and Solar Module Prices
Driven by technological advancements, 
manufacturing scale and global oversupply, solar 
module prices have declined sharply from around 
USD 1.8/W in 2010 to nearly USD 0.1/W, improving the 
economics of utility-scale solar projects. At the same 
time, India’s solar market is increasingly shaped by 
domestic-content requirements. ALMM List-I covers 
solar PV modules, while ALMM List-II covers solar PV 
cells; the Government has also initiated measures 
relating to approved manufacturers for upstream 
components such as wafers and ingots.36 For ACME 
Solar, only three projects currently have ALMM List-II 
applicability — the SECI FDRE projects with tariffs 
of INR 6/kWh, the SJVN FDRE projects with tariffs of 
INR 7/kWh, and the REMCL RTC bids. The remaining 
projects are exempt from ALMM List-II requirements, 
as their bids were submitted prior to 31st August 2025.
In parallel, the phased withdrawal of Inter-State 
Transmission System (ISTS) charge waivers is 
influencing the economics of inter-state renewable 
power. Under the current framework, the waiver for 
eligible solar projects commissioned after June 2025 
reduces progressively, with applicable ISTS charges 
increasing from 25% in FY 2026 to 50% in FY 2027, 
75% in FY 2028 and 100% thereafter. The Government 
has also clarified that eligible projects delayed 
due to transmission-system unavailability can 
retain the applicable graded waiver, subject to 
specified conditions.
The extension of the waiver mechanism for eligible 
projects facing transmission delays provides 
greater clarity to DISCOMs and can help protect the 
economics of contracted projects. For ACME Solar, 
this creates an opportunity for eligible off-takers 
to avail the applicable ISTS waiver where General 
Network Access (GNA) or transmission infrastructure 
is delayed, supporting the competitiveness of the 
Company’s contracted projects.
These policy dynamics, alongside declining 
technology costs, continue to shape tariff 
competitiveness and procurement decisions 
in India’s renewable energy market. In major 
government auctions during FY 2026, including those 
conducted by GUVNL, discovered tariffs reached INR 
2.34/kWh, with project-specific factors such as grid 
connectivity and state regulations resulting in tariffs 
of up to INR 3.05/kWh.37
Fiscal and Policy Incentives
The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) 
has maintained its structured, annual bidding 
trajectory of 50 GW of renewable energy capacity 
(including at least 10 GW of wind) rolling through to 
FY 2027–28. This framework is specifically designed to 
meet the nation’s ambitious 500 GW non-fossil 
fuel capacity target by 2030.38 Furthermore, 
the successful operational integration of core 
central-level allocations, such as the Jawaharlal 
Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM) pathways, 
alongside the continuous infrastructure expansion of 
dedicated ultra-mega solar parks, underscores the 
government’s sustained focus on solar power as the 
primary driver of its national energy transition.
Domestic supply chain resilience has been 
significantly strengthened by the Production 
Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. Under the National 
Programme on High Efficiency Solar PV Modules, a 
dedicated fiscal allocation of INR 240,000 million 
has driven massive gigawatt-scale capacity setup 
across the upstream manufacturing value chain.39 
By the close of FY 2026, India’s cumulative domestic 
solar module manufacturing capacity expanded 
rapidly to approximately 172 GW. Concurrently, the 
phased deployment of Intra-state and Inter-state 
Green Energy Corridors has scaled up to handle 
the transmission of this record high-volume clean 
generation.40

Focus on Energy Storage Systems (ESS) and 
Complex Solutions
Energy storage technologies enhance grid stability 
by storing excess energy when demand is low and 
releasing it during peak times. Lithium-based battery 
solutions are progressing quickly, with constant 
structural breakthroughs in materials, cell designs, 
manufacturing, and alternative chemistries shaping 
their utility.
Between 2020 and 2026, the cost of lithium-ion 
batteries dropped sharply, driven by technological 
improvements, lower prices of key raw materials like 
lithium, cobalt, and nickel, and a rapid expansion 
in global manufacturing capacity. Global cell costs 
have declined for Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) 
architectures and Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) 
options. This decline has significantly increased the 
commercial viability and attractiveness of Battery 
Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in power projects, 
triggering high industry participation in recent 
storage auctions. Beyond 2030, solid-state batteries 
are expected to achieve commercial availability, 
promising significant performance leaps.
The Government is actively promoting domestic 
battery manufacturing, targeting a battery 
production capacity of 200 GWh by 2030.41 This 
policy directly aligns with the strategic requirements 
mapped by the International Energy Agency (IEA) 
in its Critical Minerals Data Explorer, which provides 
global demand projections for 37 critical minerals 
needed for clean energy transitions across the 
three main IEA scenarios and 11 technology-specific 
cases.42
Beyond supply-side incentives, the sector is being 
supported by regulatory measures that are improving 
the viability and flexibility of BESS deployment. 
CTU has begun processing BESS connectivity 
applications under the Right of First Refusal (RoFR) 
framework, while allowing BESS projects to utilise 
available ISTS grid margins for charging, subject to 
applicable conditions and discharge it during non-
solar hours using the same existing transmission 
infrastructure which increases the overall utilisation 
of transmission lines. For projects opting to install 
commensurate renewable generation, the current 
framework provides up to 36 months from the 
applicable connectivity start point to commission 
the associated renewable generation for charging 
the BESS, supporting a phased approach to 
storage deployment.
The regulatory framework is also evolving to provide 
greater certainty around projects affected by 
transmission delays. CERC has proposed measures 
under its 2026 connectivity and GNA framework to 
provide additional flexibility around connectivity 
and commissioning timelines, while compensation 
mechanisms apply in specified cases. CERC has 
given regulatory certainty to those projects which 
are delayed with respect to connectivity timelines 
and allowed a period of up to 12 months beyond 
the GNA effectiveness date or start date with 
compensation charges. Separately, the Ministry of 
Power has provided for extension of applicable ISTS 
waiver benefits where projects are delayed due to 
transmission connectivity, subject to the relevant 
commissioning slabs and conditions.
Taking cognisance of the fact that BESS projects 
can commission much earlier as compared to 
its associated RE for charging, MNRE and MoP has 
also clarified that wherever BESS component is 
commissioned prior to SCOD but its RE is under-
construction, the developers can utilise such BESS 
for merchant sale of power using conventional grid 
power without requiring consent or NOC from REIA/
buying entity. Thus, it creates opportunity for those 
projects where grid substation is either operational 
or bay is charged for BESS component as BESS 
can be deployed in merchant mode ahead of the 
associated renewable capacity, enabling storage 
assets to generate cash flows while grid connectivity 
for the broader project is being established. 
Concurrently, interest has surged in standalone ESS 
projects and integrated configurations such as Firm 
and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) and 
Round-the-Clock (RTC) projects.

Management Discussion and Analysis
FDRE projects deliver reliable, on-demand power 
by integrating variable solar and wind with energy 
storage systems. This configuration ensures a 
consistent supply of electricity, even when natural 
conditions are unfavourable, enhancing grid stability 
and reducing reliance on fossil fuels. RTC projects 
take this further by guaranteeing 24/7 power 
availability through a mix of renewable sources 
and storage, often complemented by flexible 
generation assets. These models are pivotal in India’s 
transition to a low-carbon energy system, offering 
utilities and industries dependable green power at 
competitive tariffs.
In recent large-scale allocations, out of a total 77 
GW of competitive bids, solar projects accounted 
for roughly 60 GW. and wind projects made up 
remaining 17 GW.43
Availability of Low-cost Financing
Low-cost financing is crucial for India to deploy 
utility-scale renewable energy and hit its 500 GW 
non-fossil fuel capacity target by 2030. To drive this, 
the government granted the clean energy sector 
Priority Sector Lending (PSL) status. Dedicated public 
financial institutions, specifically REC, PFC, IREDA, 
SBI and NaBFID, provide easy access to large-scale 
capital at competitive interest rates. Backed by its 
Navratna status, IREDA’s loan book expanded 22% 
to cross a record INR 93,075 crores by the close of 
FY 2026, proving a massive scaling up of active green 
infrastructure credit.44 
International partnerships, leveraged during 
India’s G20 Presidency and expanding through 
contemporary BRICS and global clean energy 
frameworks, increasingly focus on blended finance 
models and multilateral funding. These instruments 
are designed to de-risk capital injections into 
emerging technologies like offshore wind, green 
hydrogen, and battery storage.
Technological Advancements
The solar power sector continues to achieve 
significant efficiency gains driven by rapid 
technological advancements across module design 
and cell architecture. In particular, the industry-
wide adoption of bifacial module designs, utilising 
dual-pane glass construction or reflective back 
sheets, allows modules to capture light from both 
sides, optimising power generation and maximising 
overall energy yield while minimising land and 
resource consumption.
Simultaneously, global cell manufacturing is 
transitioning rapidly toward Tunnel Oxide Passivated 
Contact (TOPCon) technology.45 By delivering higher 
conversion efficiencies and lower temperature 
degradation compared to traditional P-type cells, 
TOPCon enables superior energy capture. Furthermore, 
because TOPCon manufacturing processes can be 
integrated into legacy Passivated Emitter and Rear 
Cell (PERC) production lines with minimal capital 
equipment upgrades, it has emerged as the prevailing 
standard for utility-scale solar expansion.46
As the country moves towards self-reliance in solar 
manufacturing, India’s cumulative domestic solar 
module manufacturing capacity expanded rapidly 
to approximately 172 GW by the close of FY 2026.47 
Reflecting this growth, solar cell and module imports 
dropped by 2.8% y-o-y during the Q1 cycle.48 The 
industry is systematically transitioning from older 
p-type architectures to high-efficiency n-type solar 
cell technologies (including TOPCon, Heterojunction 
Technology (HJT), and back contact designs), 
which deliver higher cell efficiency and overall cost 
reductions despite material intensity challenges 
regarding critical mineral inputs.
Favourable Conditions for Wind capacity
India’s wind energy sector continued to expand in 
FY 2026, with cumulative installed capacity crossing 
56 GW and approximately 6.05 GW added during the 
year. Policy support, including the Wind Renewable 
Consumption Obligation and growing adoption of 
wind-solar hybrid projects, continues to support the 
sector’s development. For ACME Solar, wind remains 
a complementary technology within its diversified 
renewable energy portfolio, supporting hybrid and 
firm, dispatchable renewable energy solutions 
alongside solar and BESS.

ESOP Scheme were proposed to be extended to 
eligible employees of the subsidiary(ies) and/or 
holding company(ies) of the Company by way of 
a separate shareholders’ resolution.
	
Subsequently, the members of the Company 
approved (a) the above-mentioned amendments 
to the ESOP Scheme and (b) grant of options to 
the eligible employees of the subsidiary(ies) 
and/or holding company(ies) of the Company 
under the ESOP Scheme, through postal ballot on 
12th June 2026.
	
During the FY 2026, Company has granted 3,911,414 
stock options under the ESOP Scheme. A detailed 
report with respect to options exercised, vested, 
lapsed, exercise price, vesting period is annexed 
as Annexure E to this report. Further, the ESOP 
Scheme is in compliance with SEBI (Share Based 
Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 
2021 (“SEBI SBEB Regulations”). The Company 
formed an irrevocable trust under the name 
and style of “ACME Employees Welfare Trust” 
for the purpose of administration of the ESOP 
Scheme. The ESOP Scheme is implemented and 
administered through a trust route for extending 
the benefits to the eligible employees.
	
The certificate from the Secretarial Auditor of 
the Company, that the ESOP Scheme has been 
implemented in accordance with the SEBI SBEB 
Regulations along with the resolutions passed by 
the Members, would be available for electronic 
inspection by the Members at the ensuing 
11th AGM.
	
Further, the details specified under Regulation 14 
of the SEBI SBEB Regulations, are available on the 
Company’s website at

renewable (hybrid/FDRE) projects that aid grid decarbonisation; (iii) progressive replacement of diesel gensets 
with solar/battery back-up at sites; and (iv) energy-efficiency measures across offices and O&M facilities.

Report on Corporate Governance
At ACME Solar Holdings Limited (“Company”), corporate 
governance is an integral part of the way we conduct 
our business. It is founded on the principles of integrity, 
transparency, accountability and fairness, and serves 
as the foundation for responsible decision-making 
and sustainable value creation. We believe that strong 
governance is not defined solely by compliance with 
laws and regulations, but by consistently acting 
in the best interests of our shareholders and all 
other stakeholders.
Our governance framework has been developed to 
support the Company’s long-term strategy while 
ensuring effective oversight, prudent risk management 
and ethical business conduct. Clearly defined roles, 
robust internal controls and structured decision-
making processes enable us to operate responsibly 
and respond effectively to an evolving business and 
regulatory environment.
The Board of Directors provides strategic leadership and 
oversees the Company’s performance, governance 
practices and risk management framework. It is 
supported by various Board Committees, each 
entrusted with specific responsibilities relating to audit, 
risk management, nomination and remuneration, 
stakeholder relationships and corporate social 
responsibility & sustainability. Together, the Board and 
its Committees promote informed decision-making, 
independent oversight and balanced governance 
across the organisation.
We recognise that effective governance extends 
beyond financial oversight. Accordingly, the Company 
has established systems for internal controls, cyber 
security, data protection and information security. 
These systems are periodically reviewed and 
strengthened through independent assessments and 
continuous monitoring to address emerging risks and 
changing regulatory expectations.
The Company remains committed to maintaining 
transparent and timely communication with investors, 
regulators and other stakeholders. We endeavour 
to provide accurate, complete and meaningful 
disclosures relating to our financial performance, 
material developments, related party transactions 
and other matters that may influence stakeholder 
decisions. Our disclosure practices are aligned with the 
requirements of the Securities and Exchange Board of 
India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI Listing Regulations”), 
Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”) and other applicable laws 
and regulations.
Company’s Philosophy on Corporate 
Governance
The Company’s approach to corporate governance 
is guided by the belief that responsible business 
practices are essential for sustainable growth. Our 
governance philosophy is built upon the values of 
integrity, transparency, fairness, accountability and 
professionalism. These values shape our decisions, 
strengthen stakeholder confidence and support the 
creation of long-term value.
Compliance with applicable laws, regulations and 
governance standards is a fundamental responsibility. 
At the same time, we endeavour to foster a culture 
where ethical conduct, sound judgement and 
responsible decision-making become an integral 
part of everyday business practices rather than 
merely fulfilling statutory obligations.
To reinforce this commitment, the Company has 
adopted comprehensive policies and governance 
mechanisms covering areas such as prevention 
of 
insider 
trading, 
related 
party 
transactions, 
whistleblower protection, enterprise risk management, 
information security and regulatory compliance. 
These frameworks encourage transparency, promote 
accountability and support a culture of integrity 
across all levels of the organisation.
We believe that corporate governance is most effective 
when it is embedded in the organisational culture. Every 
employee, member of management and Director shares 
the responsibility of upholding the Company’s values and 
maintaining the trust placed in us by our stakeholders.

Impairment assessment of carrying values of investments in 
and loans given to subsidiaries
Refer note 2.1(m) and 2.1(g) in material accounting policy 
information and note 6 and 15 in notes forming part of 
standalone financial statements in relation to investments in 
and loans to subsidiaries.
As at 31st March 2026, the Company has investments in and 
loans given to subsidiaries aggregating to INR 75,623.99 million, 
which constitutes 58.43% of the total assets of the Company.
At each period end, the management reviews whether any 
impairment indicators exist in the carrying value of investments, 
in accordance with the requirements of Ind AS 36, “Impairment 
of Assets” (‘Ind AS 36’), and whether there is any significant 
increase in credit risk in loans receivables in accordance with 
the requirements of Ind AS 109, “Financial instruments” (‘Ind AS 
109’). In respect of investments and loans where impairment 
indicators are identified or significant increase in credit risk is 
noted, the management performs a detailed impairment test 
by determining the recoverable value of such balances.
As at 31st March 2026, the carrying value of investment in 14 
subsidiaries was higher than their net worth, which has been 
identified as an impairment indicator by the management in 
accordance with Ind AS 36.
The management has estimated the recoverable amount of its 
investment in such subsidiaries using the ‘Discounted Cash Flow 
valuation model’. The future cash flows were projected based 
on the Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) entered with the 
customers for a long term and the present value of such cash 
flows were derived using a discount rate.
As per such assessment done by the management, no 
further adjustments are required to the carrying value of the 
investments in and loans given to such subsidiaries as at 
31st March 2026.
Considering the significance of aforesaid balances to the overall 
financial statements, the large number of entities and degree of 
judgement involved in assumptions used for the computation 
of the recoverable amount, we have considered impairment 
assessment of carrying value of investments in and loans given 
to subsidiaries as a key audit matter for the current year audit.
Our audit procedures in relation to impairment assessment 
of the carrying values of investments in and loans given to 
subsidiaries included, but were not limited to the following:
•	 Obtained an understanding of the management’s process 
for identification of impairment indicators for investments 
and significant increase in credit risk of loans, and evaluated 
the design and tested the operating effectiveness of key 
internal financial controls relating to such process;
•	 Evaluated the Company’s accounting policies with 
respect to impairment assessment and assessed its 
compliance with the requirements of Ind AS 36 and 
Ind AS 109;
•	 Obtained the management’s assessment on impairment 
indicators around the recoverability of investment in and 
loans given to subsidiaries and tested the mathematical 
accuracy of the underlying calculations and traced such 
information to source financial information relating to 
subsidiary companies;
•	 For cases where impairment indicators presents, obtained 
the impairment assessment working from the management 
and tested the arithmetical accuracy of valuation model 
and traced the future cash flow projections used for 
determining recoverable amount with the approved 
business plans and signed PPAs entered with the customers;
•	 Performed sensitivity analysis of the key assumptions, 
including the discount rate applied in determining the 
recoverable value to evaluate the possible variation on the 
current recoverable amount to ascertain the sufficiency of 
headroom available;
•	 Reviewed the regularity of repayment of principal and 
payments of interest as per terms of the agreement relating 
to loans given to the subsidiary companies; and
•	 Evaluated the appropriateness and adequacy of disclosures 
given in the standalone financial statements in accordance 
with applicable accounting standards.

1. i)	 Corporate information
	
ACME Solar Holdings Limited "(the Company)" 
was incorporated as of 03rd June 2015 under the 
Companies Act, 2013. The Company is domiciled 
in India with its registered office situated at Plot 
152, Sector 44, Gurugram, Haryana – 122002, India.
	
The Company, together with its subsidiaries, 
are engaged in the business of establishing, 
commissioning, 
setting 
up, 
operating 
and 
maintaining power generation using solar, fossil 
and alternate source of energy and act as owners, 
manufacturers, engineers, procurers, buyers, 
sellers, distributors, dealers and contractors 
for setting up of power plant using glass bases 
mirrors, photo voltaic, boilers, turbines and/or 
other equipments for generating, distribution 
and supplying of electricity and other products 
using solar, fossil and alternate source of energy 
under conditions of direct ownership or through 
its affiliates, associates or subsidiaries. On 
22nd June 2024, the Company has been 
converted from Private Limited Company to 
Public Limited Company.
	
During the previous year, the Company has 
completed an Initial Public Offer ("IPO") of 
100,353,919 Equity shares having face value of 
INR 2 each at INR 289 per equity share (including 
share premium of INR 287 per share), comprising 
(i) offer for sale of 17,474,048 equity shares 
by selling shareholders and (ii) fresh issue of 
82,879,871 equity shares. The equity shares of the 
Company were listed on BSE Limited (‘BSE’) and 
National Stock Exchange of India Limited ('NSE') on 
13th November 2024.
	
The financial statement have been authorised for 
issue by the Board of Directors on 07th May 2026.
2.1	 Material accounting policies
a)	
Basis of preparation
	
The standalone financial statements have been 
prepared in accordance with Indian Accounting 
Standards (Ind AS) notified under Section 133 read 
with Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 
(Amendment) Rules, 2016 and the relevant 
provisions of the Act. Accounting policies have 
been consistently applied except where a newly 
issued accounting standard is initially adopted 
or a revision to an existing accounting standard 
requires a change in the accounting policy 
hitherto in use.
	
The financial statements are presented in INR 
and all values are rounded to the nearest million 
except where otherwise indicated.
	
Historical cost convention
	
The 
standalone 
financial 
statements 
have 
been prepared on a historical cost convention 
on a going concern basis except for certain 
financial assets and financial liabilities which are 
measured at fair value.
b)	
Use of estimates
	
The 
preparation 
of 
financial 
statement 
in 
conformity with Ind AS requires the management 
to make judgments, estimates and assumptions 
that affect the reported amounts of revenues,

h)	
Income taxes
	
Tax expense recognised in profit or loss comprises 
the sum of deferred tax and current tax. Current 
and deferred tax is recognised in profit or loss, 
except to the extent that it relates to items 
recognised in other comprehensive income 
or directly in equity. In this case, the tax is also 
recognised in other comprehensive income or 
directly in equity, respectively.
	
Current tax
	
Current tax is measured at the amount expected 
to be paid using the tax laws that have been 
enacted 
or 
substantively 
enacted 
by 
the 
end of the reporting period and includes any 
adjustment to tax payable in respect of previous 
years. The carrying amounts of deferred tax are 
reviewed at the end of each reporting period on 
the basis of its most likely amount and adjusted 
if needed. Assessing the most likely amount of 
current and deferred tax in case of uncertainties 
(e.g. as a result of the need to interpreting the 
requirements of the applicable tax law), requires 
the Company to apply judgments in considering 
whether it is probable that the taxation authority 
will accept the tax treatment retained. The 
Company measures its tax balances either based 
on the most likely amount or the expected value, 
depending on which method provides a better 
prediction of the resolution of the uncertainty."
	
Deferred tax
	
Deferred income taxes are calculated using the 
liability method on temporary differences arising 
between the tax bases of assets and liabilities 
and their carrying amounts in the financial 
statements. Deferred income tax is measured 
using tax rates and tax laws that have been 
enacted or substantively enacted by the end of 
the reporting period and are expected to apply 
when the related asset is realised or the liability 
is settled. Deferred income tax is not accounted 
for if it arises from initial recognition of an asset 
or liability in a transaction other than a business 
combination that at the time of the transaction 
affects neither accounting profit nor taxable 
profit (tax loss).
	
Deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent 
it is probable that the underlying tax loss or 
deductible temporary difference will be utilised 
against future taxable income. This is assessed 
based on the Company's forecast of future 
operating results, adjusted for significant non-
taxable income and expenses and specific 
limits on the use of any unused tax loss or credit. 
The carrying amounts of deferred tax assets 
(including minimum alternate tax(MAT) credit 
entitlement) are reviewed at the end of each 
reporting period and adjusted to the extent that it 
is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profit 
will be available to allow the benefit of part or all 
of that deferred tax asset to be utilised.
	
Deferred tax liabilities are generally recognised 
in full, although Ind AS 12 specifies limited 
exemptions. As a result of these exemptions 
the Company does not recognise deferred tax 
on temporary differences relating to goodwill. 
Deferred tax liabilities are recognised on taxable 
temporary differences arising on investments 
in subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates, 
except where the Company is able to control 
the reversal of the temporary difference and it is 
probable that the temporary difference will not 
reverse in the foreseeable future. The Company 
does not offset deferred tax assets and liabilities 
unless it has a legally enforceable right to set off 
current tax assets against current tax liabilities 
and the deferred tax relates to the same taxable 
entity and levied by same taxation authority.

to owners are not depreciated or amortised.
	
For these purposes, sale transactions include 
exchanges of non-current assets for other 
non-current assets when the exchange has 
commercial substance. The criteria for held for 
sale classification is regarded met only when 
the assets or disposal group is available for 
immediate sale in its present condition, subject 
only to terms that are usual and customary for 
sales/distribution of such assets (or disposal 
groups), its sale is highly probable; and it will 
genuinely be sold, not abandoned.
(q)	 Foreign currency
	
a)	
Functional and presentation currency
	
	
The standalone financial statements are 
presented in Indian Rupee ('INR'), which is also 
the functional currency of the Company and 
presentation currency for the standalone 
financial statements.
	
b)	
Foreign currency transactions and 
balances
	
	
Foreign currency transactions are translated 
into the functional currency, using the 
exchange rates prevailing at the dates of the 
transactions (spot exchange rate). Foreign 
exchange gains and losses resulting from 
the settlement of such transactions and 
from the remeasurement of monetary items 
denominated in foreign currency at period-
end exchange rates are recognised in profit 
or loss.

new standards or amendments to the existing 
standards under Companies (Indian Accounting 
Standards) Rules as issued from time to time.

2.2	 Significant management judgement 
in applying accounting policies and 
estimation uncertainty
	
When 
preparing 
the 
financial 
statement, 
management makes a number of judgements, 
estimates and assumptions about the recognition 
and measurement of assets, liabilities, income 
and expenses.
	
Deferred tax assets
	
A deferred tax asset is recognised to the extent 
that it is probable that future taxable profit 
will be available against which the deductible 
temporary differences and tax losses can be 
utilised. Accordingly, the Company exercises 
its judgement to reassess the carrying amount 
of deferred tax assets at the end of each 
reporting period.
	
Impairment of non-financial assets
	
In 
assessing 
impairment, 
management 
estimates the recoverable amount of each asset 
or cash-generating units based on expected 
future cash flows and uses an interest rate to 
discount them. Estimation uncertainty relates to 
assumptions about future operating results and 
the determination of a suitable discount rate.
	
Fair value measurement
	
When the fair value of financial assets and 
financial liabilities recorded in the balance 
sheet cannot be measured based on quoted 
prices in active markets, their fair value is 
measured using valuation techniques including 
the Discounted Cash Flow model. The inputs to 
these models are taken from observable markets 
where possible, but where this is not feasible, a 
degree of judgement is required in establishing 
fair values. Judgements include considerations 
of inputs such as liquidity risk, credit risk and 
volatility. Changes in assumptions about these 
factors could affect the reported fair value of 
financial instruments.
	
Revenue recognition
	
For performance obligation satisfied over time, 
the revenue recognition is done by measuring 
the progress towards complete satisfaction 
of performance obligation. The progress is 
measured in terms of a proportion of actual 
cost incurred to-date, to the total estimated cost 
attributable to the performance obligation.

19th September 2017. These CCDs were unsecured and their holders were not entitled to have any claim on any

at any time at the option of CCD holders and the Company after the date of allotment. In case no option were

thirty years from the date of allotment. Each CCD along with interest were mandatorily converted to 1.0444158 
equity share of INR 10 each at a price of INR 957.47 (inclusive of premium of INR 947.47) subject to ignoring of

Note 39 Employee benefit
Defined contribution
Contributions are made to the recognised provident and family pension fund, cover all eligible employees under 
applicable Acts. Both the employees and the Company make pre-determined contributions to the provident 
fund. The contributions are normally based upon a proportion of the employee’s salary. The Company has 
recognised in Statement of profit and loss an amount of INR 98.90 million (31st March 2025: INR 55.01 million) 
towards employer’s contribution in provident fund and other funds in the Statement of profit and loss.
Defined benefit obligation
Provision for gratuity, payable to eligible employees on retirement/separation is based upon an actuarial 
valuation as at the year ended 31st March 2026. Major drivers in actuarial assumptions, typically, are years of 
service and employee compensation. The commitments are actuarially determined using the ‘Projected Unit 
Credit Method’ as at the period end. Gains/losses on changes in actuarial assumptions are accounted in Other 
Comprehensive Income as identified by the management of the Company.
Other long term employee benefits
Provision for unfunded compensated absences payable to eligible employees on availment/retirement/
separation, is based upon an actuarial valuation as at the year ended 31st March 2026. Major drivers in actuarial 
assumptions, typically, are years of service and employee compensation. The commitments are actuarially 
determined using the ‘Projected Unit Credit Method’ as at the period end. Gains/losses on changes in actuarial 
assumptions are accounted in Other Comprehensive Income.

Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 inserted by the Companies (Accounts) Amendment Rules 
2021 requiring companies, which uses accounting software for maintaining its books of account, shall use only 
such accounting software which has a feature of recording audit trail of each and every transaction, creating 
an edit log of each change made in the books of account along with the date when such changes were made 
and ensuring that the audit trail cannot be disabled.

trail feature enabled at the database level to capture direct data changes made in the accounting software 
used for maintenance of accounting records. There is no instance of audit trail feature being tampered with in 
respect of the accounting software where such feature is enabled. The Company is assessing the feasibility of

Additions to capital work-in-progress and capitalisation of 
property, plant and equipment
Refer notes 2(g) for material accounting policy information 
and 3 and 6 in notes forming part of consolidated financial 
statements in relation to property, plant and equipment (‘PPE’) 
and capital work-in-progress (‘CWIP’).
During the year ended 31st March 2026, the Group has incurred 
INR 63,964.82 million towards addition to CWIP and capitalised 
INR 34,045.43 million of PPE towards commissioning of various 
power plants across six subsidiaries, aggregating to a total 
installed capacity of 450 MW of solar and wind, along with 
Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity of 1,157 MWh.
The above additions and commissioning of power plants being 
non-recurring in nature, required significant management 
efforts and judgement to identify the eligible costs which 
meet the recognition criteria under Ind AS 16 “Property, Plant 
and Equipment” (‘Ind AS 16’), including allocation of overheads 
and employee costs to capital projects, determine timing of 
capitalisation, estimate related useful lives and assign residual 
values to additions made to PPE.
Further, such capital expenditure has been funded from the 
specific borrowings raised. Accordingly, the borrowing cost 
incurred on such borrowings have been capitalised as part of 
cost of the assets in accordance with the principles of Ind AS 
23, Borrowing Costs (‘Ind AS 23)’.
Considering the magnitude of overall capital expenditure 
and efforts and judgements involved as mentioned above, 
we have considered addition to capital work-in-progress and 
capitalisation of property, plant and equipment as a key audit 
matter for the current year audit.

work-in-progress and capitalisation of property, plant and 
equipment included, but not limited to the following:

assessed the appropriateness of the Group’s material 
accounting policy information on property, plant and 
equipment and capital work in-progress in accordance 
with Ind AS 16; 
•	 Evaluated the design and tested the operating 
effectiveness of key internal financial controls relating to 
capitalisation of various costs;
•	 Performed test of details by selecting samples of additions 
during the year, and verified the underlying supporting 
documents including contracts, agreements and invoices 
to ensure such items are recorded accurately in the correct 
period, in accordance with the requirements of Ind AS 16; 
•	 Assessed appropriateness of timing of capitalisation and 
examined the useful lives considered for calculation of 
depreciation charge as per technical evaluation provided 
by the management;
•	 Obtained the project completion/handover certificate 
provided by the management for projects commissioned 
during the year, to determine whether the asset is in the 
location and condition necessary for it to be capable of 
operating in the manner intended by the management;
•	 Assessed reasonableness and appropriateness of 
allocation of overhead and employee costs to capital 
projects;
•	 Assessed that the borrowing cost capitalised during the 
year is in accordance with the accounting policy of the 
Group and Ind AS 23; and
•	 Evaluated the appropriateness and adequacy of the 
disclosures given in the consolidated financial statements 
in accordance with the applicable accounting standards.

Independent Auditor’s Report on the internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements under Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 
of Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013  
(‘the Act’)
1.	
In conjunction with our audit of the consolidated 
financial statements of ACME Solar Holdings 
Limited (formerly known as ACME Solar Holdings 
Private Limited) (‘the Holding Company’) and 
its subsidiaries (the Holding Company and its 
subsidiaries together referred to as ‘the Group’) 
as at and for the year ended 31st March 2026, we 
have audited the internal financial controls with 
reference to financial statements of the Holding 
Company and its subsidiary companies, which 
are companies covered under the Act, as at 
that date.
Responsibilities of Management and Those 
Charged with Governance for Internal 
Financial Controls
2.	
The respective Board of Directors of the Holding 
Company and its subsidiary companies, which 
are companies covered under the Act, are 
responsible for establishing and maintaining 
internal financial controls based on the internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements criteria established by the Company 
considering the essential components of internal 
control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of 
Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting 
issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants 
of India (‘ICAI’). These responsibilities include the 
design, implementation and maintenance of 
adequate internal financial controls that were 
operating effectively for ensuring the orderly and 
efficient conduct of the Company’s business, 
including adherence to the Company’s policies, 
the safeguarding of its assets, the prevention 
and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy 
and completeness of the accounting records, 
and the timely preparation of reliable financial 
information, as required under the Act.
Auditor’s Responsibility for the Audit of the 
Internal Financial Controls with Reference to 
Financial Statements
3.	
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on 
the internal financial controls with reference to 
financial statements of the Holding Company 
and its subsidiary companies as aforesaid, 
based on our audit. We conducted our audit 
in accordance with the Standards on Auditing 
issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants 
of India (‘ICAI’) prescribed under Section 143(10) 
of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit 
of internal financial controls with reference to 
financial statements, and the Guidance Note on 
Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial 
Reporting (‘the Guidance Note’) issued by the ICAI. 
Those Standards and the Guidance Note require 
that we comply with ethical requirements and 
plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable 
assurance about whether adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements were established and maintained 
and if such controls operated effectively in all 
material respects.
4.	
Our audit involves performing procedures to 
obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of 
the internal financial controls with reference 
to financial statements and their operating 
effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial 
controls with reference to financial statements 
includes obtaining an understanding of such 
internal financial controls, assessing the risk 
that a material weakness exists, and testing 
and evaluating the design and operating 
effectiveness of internal control based on the 
assessed risk. The procedures selected depend 
on the auditor’s judgement, including the 
assessment of the risks of material misstatement 
of the financial statements, whether due to fraud 
or error.

5.	
We believe that the audit evidence we have 
obtained, and the audit evidence obtained by 
the other auditors in terms of their report referred 
to in the Other Matters paragraph below is 
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for 
our audit opinion on the internal financial controls 
with reference to financial statements of the

as aforesaid.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with 
Reference to Financial Statements
6.	
A company’s internal financial controls with 
reference to financial statements is a process 
designed to provide reasonable assurance 
regarding the reliability of financial reporting 
and the preparation of financial statements for 
external purposes in accordance with generally 
accepted accounting principles. A company’s 
internal financial controls with reference to 
financial statements include those policies and 
procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of 
records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and 
fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of 
the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable 
assurance that transactions are recorded as 
necessary to permit preparation of financial 
statements 
in 
accordance 
with 
generally 
accepted accounting principles, and that receipts 
and expenditures of the company are being 
made only in accordance with authorisations 
of management and directors of the company; 
and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding 
prevention or timely detection of unauthorised 
acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s 
assets that could have a material effect on the 
financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial 
Controls with Reference to Financial 
Statements
7.	
Because of the inherent limitations of internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements, including the possibility of collusion 
or improper management override of controls, 
material misstatements due to error or fraud 
may occur and not be detected. Also, projections 
of any evaluation of the internal financial controls 
with reference to financial statements to future 
periods are subject to the risk that the internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements may become inadequate because 
of changes in conditions, or that the degree of 
compliance with the policies or procedures 
may deteriorate.
Opinion
8.	
In our opinion and based on the consideration 
of the reports of the other auditors on internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements of the subsidiary companies, the 
Holding Company and its subsidiary companies, 
which are companies covered under the Act, 
have in all material respects, adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements and such controls were operating 
effectively as at 31st March 2026, based on the 
internal financial controls with reference to the 
financial statements criteria established by the 
Holding Company and its subsidiary companies 
considering the essential components of internal 
control stated in the Guidance note issued by 
the ICAI.

with reference to financial statements insofar as

Material accounting policy information
a)	
Basis of preparation
	
The consolidated financial statements have been 
prepared in accordance with Indian Accounting 
Standards (Ind AS) notified under Section 133 read 
with Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 
(Amendment) Rules, 2016 and the relevant 
provisions of the Act. Accounting policies have 
been consistently applied except where a newly 
issued accounting standard is initially adopted 
or a revision to an existing accounting standard 
requires a change in the accounting policy 
hitherto in use.
	
The 
consolidated 
financial 
statements 
are 
presented in INR and all values are rounded to the 
nearest million with two decimals except where 
otherwise indicated. 
	
Historical cost convention
	
The consolidated financial statements have 
been prepared on a historical cost convention 
on a going concern basis except for certain 
financial assets and financial liabilities which are 
measured at fair value.
b)	
Basis of consolidation
	
The Group's Consolidated financial statements 
comprise the financial statements of Holding 
Company and all of its subsidiaries as at 
31st March 2026. The financial statements of the 
entities used for the purpose of consolidation are 
drawn up to same reporting date as that of the 
Holding Company. Subsidiaries are all entities 
over which, Holding Company exercises control. 
Holding Company exercises control only if it has 
the following:
	
(i) 	 power over the entity
	
(ii) 	 exposure, or rights, to variable returns from 
its involvement with the entity; and
	
(iii) 	 the ability to use its power over the entity to 
affect the amount of its returns.
	
The difference between the cost of investment 
in subsidiaries (investee company) to the Group 
and the proportionate share in the equity of the 
investee Company as at the date of acquisition of 
stake is recognised in the Consolidated Financial 
Statements as Goodwill or Capital Reserve, as the 
case may be. Goodwill arising on consolidation 
is tested for impairment at the Balance Sheet 
date. Non-controlling interests which represent 
part of the net profit or loss and net assets of 
subsidiaries that are not, directly or indirectly, 
owned or controlled by the Group, are excluded 
for the purpose of calculation of goodwill/
capital reserve.
	
The financial statements of the companies under 
the Group are consolidated on a line-by-line 
basis and intra-group balances and transactions

Business combinations
	
Business 
combinations 
are 
accounted 
for 
using the acquisition method. The acquisition 
method involves the recognition of the acquiree's 
identifiable 
assets 
and 
liabilities, 
including 
contingent liabilities, regardless of whether they 
were recorded in the financial statements prior to 
acquisition. On initial recognition, the assets and 
liabilities of the acquired subsidiary are included 
in the consolidated balance sheet at their fair 
values, which are also used as the bases for 
subsequent measurement in accordance with 
the Group's accounting policies. Goodwill is stated 
after separating out identifiable intangible assets. 
Goodwill represents the excess of acquisition 
cost over the fair value of the Group's share of 
the identifiable net assets of the acquiree at the 
date of acquisition. Any excess of identifiable net 
assets over acquisition cost is recognised in the 
other comprehensive income on the acquisition 
date and accumulated in equity as capital 
reserve. Acquisition related costs are accounted 
for as expenses in the period in which they are 
incurred and the services are received.
	
Business combination in which all of the 
combining entities or businesses are ultimately 
controlled by the same party or parties, both 
before and after the business combination, and 
where that control is not transitory, is referred to as 
business combinations of entities under common 
control. The accounting policy of the Group is to 
account for the assets and liabilities of acquired 
entities at their book values in its consolidated 
financial statements. The book value of the assets 
and liabilities of an acquired entity is the book 
value as reflected in the standalone financial 
statements. The excess of the fair value of the 
consideration paid (in cash and in kind) over the 
acquirer’s proportionate share of the net asset 
value acquired is adjusted in other equity. The 
consolidated financial statements and financial 
information presented for comparative year are 
since the date of existence of common control.
