e)	
Revenue from contracts with customers
	
Revenue from contracts with customers is 
recognised when control of the goods or services 
are transferred to the customer at an amount 
that reflects the consideration to which the 
Group expects to be entitled in exchange for 
those goods or services. Revenue excludes taxes 
collected on behalf of government.
	
(e.1) Sale of power
	
i)	
Revenue from sale of power is recognized 
when 
persuasive 
evidence 
of 
an 
arrangement exists, the fee is fixed or 
determinable, solar energy kilowatts are 
supplied and collectability is reasonably 
assured. Revenue is based on the solar 
energy 
kilowatts 
actually 
supplied 
to 
customers multiplied by the rate per kilo-
watt hour agreed to in the respective power 
purchase agreement (PPAs). The solar 
energy kilowatts supplied by the Group are 
validated by the customer prior to billing 
and recognition of revenue.
	
ii)	
Where Power Purchase Agreement's (PPAs) 
include scheduled rate changes, revenue 
is recognized at lower of the amount billed 
or by applying the average rate to the 
energy output estimated over the term of 
the PPA. The determination of the lesser 
amount is undertaken annually based on 
the cumulative amount that would have 
been recognized had each method been 
consistently applied from the beginning 
of the contract term. The Group estimates 
the total kilowatt hour units expected to 
be generated over the entire term of the 
PPA. The contractual rates are applied to 
this annual estimate to determine the total 
estimated revenue over the term of the PPA. 
The Group then uses the total estimated 
revenue and the total estimated kilo-watt 
hours to compute the average rate used to 
record revenue on the actual energy output 
supplied. The difference between actual 
billing and revenue recognised is recorded 
as unearned revenue.
	
(e.2) Interest income
	
	
Interest income is recorded using the 
effective interest rate (EIR). EIR is the rate that 
exactly discounts the estimated future cash 
payments or receipts over the expected life of 
the financial instrument or a shorter period, 
where appropriate, to the gross carrying 
amount of the financial asset or to the 
amortized cost of the financial liability. When 
calculating the effective interest rate, the 
Group estimates the expected cash flows by 
considering all the contractual terms of the 
financial instrument but does not consider 
the expected credit losses. Interest income is 
included in other income in the Statement of 
Profit and Loss.
	
(e.3) Claims
	
	
Claims i.e. late payment interest recoverable 
from 
customer, 
insurance 
claim 
and 
liquidated damages, are recognised on 
acceptance or actual receipt of the claim, 
whichever is earlier, considering the certainty 
as to measurement or ultimate collectability 
of revenue.
(f)	 Borrowing costs
	
Borrowing costs directly attributable to the 
acquisitions, construction or production of a 
qualifying asset are capitalised during the 
period of time that is necessary to complete 
and prepare the asset for its intended use or 
sale. Other borrowing costs are expensed in the 
period in which they are incurred and reported in 
finance costs.
(g)	 Property, plant and equipment
	
Property, plant and equipment's are carried at 
cost less accumulated depreciation. The cost 
of items of the property, plant and equipment 
comprises its purchase price net of any trade 
discount and rebate, any import duties and other 
taxes (other than those subsequently recoverable 
from tax authorities), any directly attributable 
expenditure on making the asset ready for its 
intended use, other incidental expenses and 
interest on borrowings attributable to acquisition 
of qualifying property, plant and equipments up 
to the date the asset is ready for its intended use.
	
Whenever significant parts of the property, plant 
and equipment are required to be replaced at 
intervals, the Group depreciates them separately 
based on their specific useful lives. All other 
repair and maintenance costs are recognised in 
statement of profit and loss as incurred.
	
Depreciation is recognised based on the cost 
of assets (other than freehold land) using the 
straight-line method. The useful life of property, 
plant and equipment is considered based on 
life prescribed in schedule II to the Companies

(i)	
Leased assets and right of use
	
The Group assesses at contract inception 
whether a contract is, or contains, a lease. A lease 
is defined as ‘a contract, or part of a contract, that 
conveys the right to use an asset (the underlying 
asset) for a period of time in exchange for 
consideration’.
	
To apply this definition, the Group assesses 
whether the contract meets three key evaluations 
which are whether:
•	 the contract contains an identified asset, which 
is either explicitly identified in the contract or 
implicitly specified by being identified at the 
time the asset is made available to the Group.
•	 the Group has the right to obtain substantially 
all of the economic benefits from use of the 
identified asset throughout the period of use, 
considering its rights within the defined scope 
of the contract.
•	 the Group has the right to direct the use of the 
identified asset throughout the period of use. 
The Group assess whether it has the right to 
direct ‘how and for what purpose’ the asset is 
used throughout the period of use.
	
At lease commencement date, the Group 
recognizes a right-of-use asset and a lease 
liability on the balance sheet. The right-of-use 
asset is measured at cost, which is made up 
of the initial measurement of the lease liability, 
any initial direct costs incurred by the Group, an 
estimate of any costs to dismantle and remove 
the asset at the end of the lease, and any 
lease payments made in advance of the lease 
commencement date (net of any incentives 
received).
	
The 
Group 
depreciates 
the 
right-of-use 
assets on a straight-line basis from the lease 
commencement date to the earlier of the end 
of the useful life of the underlying asset or the 
end of the lease term. The Group also assesses 
the right-of-use asset for impairment when such 
indicators exist.
	
At the commencement date, the Group measures 
the lease liability at the present value of the lease 
payments unpaid at that date, discounted using 
the interest rate implicit in the lease if that rate 
is readily available or the Group’s incremental 
borrowing rate.
	
Lease payments included in the measurement of 
the lease liability are made up of fixed payments 
(including in substance fixed), variable payments 
based on an index or rate, amounts expected to 
be payable under a residual value guarantee 
and payments arising from options reasonably 
certain to be exercised.
	
Subsequent to initial measurement, the liability 
will be reduced for payments made and 
increased for interest. It is remeasured to reflect 
any reassessment or modification, or if there are 
changes in in-substance fixed payments.
	
When the lease liability is remeasured, the 
corresponding adjustment is reflected in the 
right-of-use asset, or profit and loss if the right-
of-use asset is already reduced to zero or the 
adjustment relates to reduction in scope of 
the lease.

(j)	 Impairment of non-financial assets
	
For impairment assessment purposes, assets 
are grouped at the lowest levels for which there 
are largely independent cash inflows (cash-
generating units). As a result, some assets are 
tested individually for impairment and some are 
tested at cash-generating unit level. All individual 
assets or cash-generating units are tested for 
impairment whenever events or changes in 
circumstances indicate that the carrying amount 
may not be recoverable.
	
An impairment loss is recognised for the amount 
by which the asset’s (or cash-generating unit’s) 
carrying 
amount 
exceeds 
its 
recoverable 
amount, which is the higher of fair value less costs 
of disposal and value-in-use. To determine the 
value-in-use, management estimates expected 
future cash flows from each cash-generating unit 
and determines a suitable discount rate in order 
to calculate the present value of those cash flows. 
The date used for impairment testing procedures 
are directly linked to the Group’s latest approved 
budget, adjusted as necessary to exclude the 
effects of future reorganisations and asset 
enhancements. Discount factors are determined 
individually for each cash-generating unit and 
reflect current market assessments of the time 
value of money and asset-specific risk factors.
	
Impairment losses are charged in the statement

(m)	Income taxes
	
Tax expense recognised in profit or loss comprises 
the sum of deferred tax and current tax. Current 
and deferred tax is recognised in profit or loss, 
except to the extent that it relates to items 
recognised in other comprehensive income 
or directly in equity. In this case, the tax is also 
recognised in other comprehensive income or 
directly in equity, respectively.
	
Current tax
	
Current tax is measured at the amount expected 
to be paid using the tax laws that have been 
enacted or substantively enacted by the end of 
the reporting period and includes any adjustment 
to tax payable in respect of previous years. The 
carrying amounts of deferred tax are reviewed 
at the end of each reporting period on the basis 
of its most likely amount and adjusted if needed. 
Assessing the most likely amount of current and 
deferred tax in case of uncertainties (eg as a 
result of the need to interpreting the requirements 
of the applicable tax law), requires the Group 
to apply judgments in considering whether it is 
probable that the taxation authority will accept 
the tax treatment retained. The Group measures 
its tax balances either based on the most likely 
amount or the expected value, depending on 
which method provides a better prediction of the 
resolution of the uncertainty.
	
Deferred tax
	
Deferred income taxes are calculated using the 
liability method on temporary differences arising 
between the tax bases of assets and liabilities 
and their carrying amounts in the financial 
statements. Deferred income tax is measured 
using tax rates and tax laws that have been 
enacted or substantively enacted by the end of 
the reporting period and are expected to apply 
when the related asset is realised or the liability 
is settled. Deferred income tax is not accounted 
for if it arises from initial recognition of an asset 
or liability in a transaction other than a business 
combination that at the time of the transaction 
affects neither accounting profit nor taxable 
profit (tax loss).
	
Deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent 
it is probable that the underlying tax loss or 
deductible temporary difference will be utilised 
against future taxable income. This is assessed 
based on the Group’s forecast of future operating 
results, adjusted for significant non-taxable 
income and expenses and specific limits on the 
use of any unused tax loss or credit. The carrying 
amounts of deferred tax assets (including 
minimum alternate tax (MAT) credit entitlement) 
are reviewed at the end of each reporting period 
and adjusted to the extent that it is no longer 
probable that sufficient taxable profit will be 
available to allow the benefit of part or all of that 
deferred tax asset to be utilised.
	
Deferred tax liabilities are generally recognised 
in full, although Ind AS 12 specifies limited 
exemptions. As a result of these exemptions 
the Group does not recognise deferred tax on

Provisions are recognized only when there is a

associated with the present obligations as a

note unless the possibility of outflow is remote. 
Contingent assets are neither recognized nor 
disclosed. However, when realization of income is 
virtually certain, related asset is recognized.

(q)	 Earnings per share
	
Basic earnings per share are calculated by dividing 
the net profit or loss for the period attributable to 
equity shareholders (after deducting attributable 
taxes) by the weighted average number of equity 
shares outstanding during the period. Partly paid 
equity shares are treated as a fraction of an 
equity share to the extent that they are entitled 
to participate in dividends relative to a fully 
paid equity share during the reporting period. 
The weighted average number of equity shares 
outstanding during the period is adjusted for 
events such as bonus issue, bonus element in 
a rights issue, share split and reverse share split 
(consolidation of shares) that have changed the 
number of equity shares outstanding, without a 
corresponding change in resources.
	
For the purpose of calculating diluted earnings 
per share, the net profit or loss for the period 
attributable to equity shareholders and the 
weighted average number of shares outstanding 
during the period are adjusted for the effects of 
all dilutive potential equity shares.

(r)	 Investment Properties
	
Investment properties are measured initially at 
cost, including transaction costs. Subsequent 
to initial recognition, investment properties are 
stated at cost less accumulated depreciation 
and accumulated impairment loss, if any.
	
The cost includes the cost of replacing parts 
and borrowing costs for long-term construction 
projects if the recognition criteria are met. When 
significant parts of the investment properties 
are required to be replaced at intervals, the 
Group depreciates them separately based on 
their specific useful lives. All other repair and 
maintenance costs are recognised in profit or 
loss as incurred.
	
Investment properties are derecognised either 
when they have been disposed of or when 
they are permanently withdrawn from use and 
no future economic benefit is expected from 
their disposal. The difference between the net 
disposal proceeds and the carrying amount 
of the asset is recognised in profit or loss in the 
period of derecognition. In determining the 
amount of consideration from the derecognition 
of investment properties the Group considers 
the effects of variable consideration, existence 
of a significant financing component, non-cash 
consideration, and consideration payable to the 
buyer (if any).
	
Transfers are made to (or from) investment 
properties only when there is a change in use. 
Transfers between investment property, owner-
occupied property and inventories do not change 
the carrying amount of the property transferred 
and they do not change the cost of that property 
for measurement or disclosure purposes.
(s)	 Inventories
	
Inventories are stated at the lower of cost and 
net realisable value. The cost of inventories 
comprises of all costs of purchase, costs of 
conversion and other costs incurred in bringing 
the inventories to their present location and 
condition. Costs of ordinarily interchangeable 
items are assigned using the first in, first out cost 
formula. Net realisable value is the estimated 
selling price in the ordinary course of business 
less any applicable selling expenses.
(t)	 Assets held for sale
	
Non-current assets are classified as held for 
sale if their carrying amount will be recovered 
principally through a sale transaction rather 
than through continuing use. This condition is 
regarded as met only when the asset is available 
for immediate sale in its present condition subject 
only to terms that are usual and customary 
for sale of such asset and its sale is highly 
probable. Management must be committed to 
the sale, which should be expected to qualify 
for recognition as a completed sale within one 
year from the date of classification. As at each 
balance sheet date, the management reviews 
the appropriateness of such classification.
	
Non-current assets classified as held for sale are 
measured at the lower of their carrying amount 
and fair value less costs to sell. The Group treats 
sale/distribution of the asset or disposal group to 
be highly probable when:
•	 the appropriate level of management is 
committed to a plan to sell the asset (or 
disposal group),
•	 an active programme to locate a buyer and 
complete the plan has been initiated (if 
applicable),
•	 the asset (or disposal group) is being actively 
marketed for sale at a price that is reasonable 
in relation to its current fair value,
•	 the sale is expected to qualify for recognition 
as a completed sale within one year from the 
date of classification, and
•	 actions required to complete the plan indicate 
that it is unlikely that significant changes 
to the plan will be made or that the plan will 
be withdrawn.
	
Property, plant and equipment and intangible 
assets once classified as held for sale/distribution 
to owners are not depreciated or amortised.
	
For these purposes, sale transactions include 
exchanges of non-current assets for other 
non-current assets when the exchange has 
commercial substance. The criteria for held for 
sale classification is regarded met only when 
the assets or disposal group is available for 
immediate sale in its present condition, subject 
only to terms that are usual and customary for 
sales/distribution of such assets (or disposal 
groups), its sale is highly probable; and it will 
genuinely be sold, not abandoned.

that it is probable that future taxable profit will be

differences and tax losses can be utilised. 
Accordingly, the Group exercises its judgement 
to reassess the carrying amount of deferred tax 
assets at the end of each reporting period.
	
Impairment of non-financial assets
	
In 
assessing 
impairment, 
management 
estimates the recoverable amount of each asset 
or cash-generating units based on expected 
future cash flows and uses an interest rate to 
discount them. Estimation uncertainty relates to 
assumptions about future operating results and 
the determination of a suitable discount rate.
	
Fair value measurement
	
When the fair value of financial assets and 
financial liabilities recorded in the balance 
sheet cannot be measured based on quoted 
prices in active markets, their fair value is 
measured using valuation techniques including 
the Discounted Cash Flow model. The inputs to 
these models are taken from observable markets 
where possible, but where this is not feasible, a 
degree of judgement is required in establishing 
fair values. Judgements include considerations 
of inputs such as liquidity risk, credit risk and 
volatility. Changes in assumptions about these 
factors could affect the reported fair value of 
financial instruments.

The Holding Company had issued 6,500,000 compulsorily convertible debentures of INR 1,000 each to ACME 
Cleantech Solutions Private Limited. Rate of interest on these CCDs is 8% with a moratorium period of one year 
from 19th September 2017.  These CCDs were unsecured and their holders were not entitled to have any claim 
on any asset of the holding Company.  These CCDs along with interest thereon, if any, were to be converted into 
equity shares at any time at the option of CCD holders and the Holding Company after the date of allotment. 
In case no option were exercised by any CCD holders then these were to be compulsory converted into equity 
shares on expiry of thirty years from the date of allotment.  Each CCD along with interest were mandatorily 
converted to 1.0444158 equity share of INR 10 each at a price of INR 957.47 (inclusive of premium of INR 947.47) 
subject to ignoring of decimal part in rounding-off.  
CCDs holders waived the interest accrued on these compulsory convertible debentures till the date 
of conversion.

1Securities premium 
Securities premium represents premium received on issue of shares. The reserve is utilised in accordance with the provisions of the 
Companies Act, 2013.
2Capital reserve
This represents the capital reserve arisen on accounting for business combination under common control business combinations. 
The amount of capital reserve represents the difference between the consideration paid for acquisition and the share capital of 
the merged entities.
3Debenture redemption reserve
The Holding Company and its subsidiaries are required to create a Debenture Redemption Reserve out of the profits which are 
available for payment of dividend for the purpose of redemption of debentures. Accordingly debenture redemption reserve has 
been created out of profits during the year.
4Share based payment reserve 
The Holding Company has a share option scheme under which option to subscribe for the Company’s shares have been granted 
to certain executives and senior employees. The share options outstanding account is used to recognise the value of equity settled 
share based payments provided to employees, including key management personnel, as part of their remuneration. 
5Retained earnings
All the profits or losses made by the Group are transferred to retained earnings from Statement of Profit and Loss and it also includes 
pre-acquisition profits of entities acquired under common control of business combination. Remeasurement of defined benefit 
plans represents the actuarial gains/(losses) recognised in other comprehensive income.

This represents the actuarial gains/losses recognised in other comprehensive income.

(iv)	 Risk management
	
The Group’s activities expose it to credit risk, liquidity risk and market risk. The Holding Company’s board 
of directors has overall responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the Group’s risk management 
framework. This note explains the sources of risk which the entity is exposed to and how the entity manages 
the risk and the related impact in the financial statements.
	
(A)	 Credit risk
	
	
Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty fails to discharge its obligation to the Group. The Group’s 
exposure to credit risk is influenced mainly by cash and cash equivalents, trade receivables and 
financial assets measured at amortised cost. The Group continuously monitors defaults of customers 
and other counterparties and incorporates this information into its credit risk controls.

conditions and the requirements of the financial covenants. To maintain or adjust the capital

B. 	
Other Matters
	
(i) 	 One of the subsidiary company had imported solar modules without payment of import duties 
amounting to INR 2,566.08 million (31st March 2025: INR 2,566.08 million), for setting up the solar plant in 
the bonded warehouse area, as defined in the license under section 58 of the Customs Act, 1962 (‘the 
Act’), along-with permission for undertaking manufacturing or other operations in the warehouse under 
section 65 of the Act, read with Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse (no. 2) Regulations, 
2019 (‘MOOWR regulations’) dated 01st October 2019 and circular 34/2019-custom dated 01st October 2019. 
As assessed by such subsidiary company’s management, the duty deferment allowed under MOOWR 
regulations is without any time limitation and further, such regulations also allow export of the said 
capital goods after use, without payment of duty under the Act.  Based on inputs from an expert, the 
subsidiary company’s management had assessed that they shall be able to comply with the conditions 
defined in the MOOWR regulations and consequently, the resultant savings towards duties in relation to 
import of capital goods, was accounted for as per applicable Ind AS.
	
	
Another five subsidiary companies had imported solar modules during the previous years and current 
year and three subsidiary companies has imported batteries during the current year with deferment 
of import duties, as per MOOWR regulations. As assessed by the management, the duty deferment 
allowed under MOOWR regulations is without any time limitation and the subsidiary companies shall 
be able to comply with all the prescribed conditions defined in the MOOWR regulations. Consequently, 
such subsidiary companies as at 31st March 2026 has accounted for the resultant benefit as per 
applicable Ind AS and is carrying 'deferred duty liability’ amounting to INR 22,587.29 million (31st March 
2025: INR 18,566.29 million).
	
	
The Central Board of Indirect taxes and Customs (CBIC) vide its instruction dated 09th July 2022 
(Instruction No.13/2022-Customs) issued to the departmental officers stated that grant of permissions 
for solar project are not in accordance with MOOWR regulation. Pertinently, there is no circular by 
CBIC regarding non-applicability of MOOWR for Battery Energy Storage System Projects (BESS). The 
Group had filed a petition before the Honourable High Court of Delhi and had been granted stay until 
the next rescheduled date of hearing.  The management based on inputs from an external expert, 
believes that the Instruction dated 09th July 2022 is principally and legally untenable and further, as 
the approval to operate under MOOWR has been granted by the authorities only after due verification 
of premises and further, as the respective subsidiaries has been complying with all the conditions 
of MOOWR regulations so far, there should not be any impact either on the already imported goods 
or on the validation of already issued licences, affecting the Group's eligibility to avail the benefits 
under the MOOWR scheme. On 06th May 2024, Honourable High Court of Delhi issued its order and 
quashed the said instruction of the CBIC dated 09th July 2022. Pursuant to the said order in favour 
of the subsidiary Companies, the custom authorities allowed import of remaining modules under 
MOOWR Scheme.  Subsequently, the custom authorities have filed an appeal against the 06th May 
2024 order before Honourable Supreme Court and the same is yet to be listed for hearing. Further, 
there is no circular or any litigation pending with respect to applicability of MOOWR for BESS projects. 
Accordingly, no adjustment is currently required in these financial statements.

Note 50 Ind AS 116 - Leases
The Group has lease agreement usually for a period of 25-30 years with individuals for land and solar park 
developers. With the exception of short-term leases and leases of low-value underlying assets, each lease is 
reflected on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. The Group classifies its right-of-use 
assets in a consistent manner to its property, plant and equipment.
Each lease generally imposes a restriction that, unless there is a contractual right for the Group to sublease 
the asset to another party, the right-of-use asset can only be used by the Group. The Group is prohibited from 
selling or pledging the underlying leased assets as security.

Reliability & Responsiveness, 
Reimagined
India’s strides toward the Viksit Bharat vision for 2047 stand at a defining crossroads 
where growth, sustainability and energy security are no longer separate journeys 
but a single, shared path forward. As our nation accelerates renewable energy 
adoption, the transition cannot realise its full potential without progressively 
replacing hydrocarbons across the economy. Today, hydrocarbons account for a 
large share of energy consumption in multiple forms — including fuels, fertilisers 
and chemicals — presenting a significant op

portunity to build a broader and more 
integrated roadmap for renewable energy growth.
As electrification expands into sectors that have traditionally relied on the flexibility 
and responsiveness of hydrocarbons, the energy system must offer comparable 
reliability, agility and responsiveness. This will require a renewable energy-led grid 
that is supported by storage, flexible generation and intelligent grid infrastructure.
Powering India’s ambition demands more than megawatts on paper; it calls 
for energy that arrives precisely when the grid calls for it, reliable in delivery and 
matched to an economy accelerating in every direction. The conversation around 
renewable energy is evolving too, moving beyond how much clean power is 
generated to how dependably it is delivered, day and night, season after season.
ACME Solar sees this shift as an invitation to lead. In FY 2026, we deepened our 
commitment to reliability by scaling our BESS* and FDRE** portfolios, weaving 
storage and flexibility into the very architecture of renewable power so that clean 
energy becomes not just abundant but unfailingly present when the moment 
demands it. We are working closely with the grid to develop solutions that can 
reliably meet short-duration and time-sensitive power demand.
With India’s Net Zero pledge by 2070 as the horizon, the path ahead calls for 
solutions that combine scale with steadfastness and vision with delivery. 
ACME Solar is architecting that future today, reimagining renewable energy not 
merely as a greener alternative but as a dependable force, one capable of 
strengthening the grid, powering ambition and steering India confidently towards 
a low-carbon tomorrow.

Dear Shareholders,
It gives me great pleasure to write 
to you about a year of impressive 
business performance even amid 
economic disruptions triggered by 
geopolitical uncertainties.

as global transition towards 
renewable energy is gaining 
fresh momentum amid growing 
geopolitical uncertainties and 
disruptions to the global oil 
trade particularly due to West 
Asia conflict. To reduce our 
exposure to external energy 
shocks and strengthen energy 
security, we need to accelerate 
the electrification of sectors 
currently dependent on 
crude oil and further scale up 
investments in sustainable and 
renewable energy.
In sync with the surge in global 
green power capacity, energy 
storage has gained significance. 
When paired with battery and 
right power electronics systems, 
renewables energy can provide 
responsive energy, grid inertia and 
long steady electricity at rates 
cheaper than fossil fuels, even 
when the sun doesn’t shine or the 
wind doesn’t blow.
Ranked among India’s leading 
renewable energy Independent 
Power Producers (IPPs), ACME Solar 
contributes significantly to the 
nation’s transition to renewables. 
Our steady rise in the clean 
energy landscape prompted us to 
focus on battery energy storage 
systems (BESS) to power the next

phase of growth.
Aligned to India’s Green 
Mission

reflects a steady progress towards 
the self-reliant, cost-effective 
energy for our people which are 
still underserved. As the country 
strides toward its Viksit Bharat vision 
for 2047, our per capita energy 
consumption needs to move from 
current ~1,500 kWh by 3x. This should 
itself be an audacious goal for all 
of us in the industry to create our 
roadmap for profitable growth.
Our goal to reach 500 GW by 2030 
itself demonstrates that India can 
think big and can charter a path 
to scale up to unprecedent levels. 
We believe that capacity created 
in the industry in the last decade 
would be very helpful for moving 
towards the Viksit Bharat target.
The evolving dynamics have 
pushed renewable power 
companies to stare at a 
transformative journey, aided by 
clear goals, agile supply chains, 
supportive policies.

energy security, affordability, and 
sustainability, the government 
plans structural policy reforms to 
align public financial flows with its 
clean energy goals.

to seizing the opportunity by 
innovating business process, plant 
configuration and technology

Storage, the New Frontier
After capacity, the next major 
step for renewable energy 
generators is storage. As batteries 
proliferate, power companies 
use them in novel ways, such 
as handling big swings in 
electricity generation from 
solar and wind farms, reducing

voltage fluctuations, frequency

and preventing blackouts 
and brownouts.

The year under review marks the 
beginning of our journey into 
BESS that serves as the base 
for our firm and dispatchable 
renewable energy (FDRE) projects. 
As India rapidly tenders 
renewable energy and storage 
capacities, the Central Electricity 
Authority estimates that 411.4 GWh 
energy storage will be needed 
by 2031-32.6 As developers 
commission all their solar and 
FDRE projects pipeline, it will create 
more duck curve situation in the 
grid which will push the evening 
and morning peak along with time 
shift in the night. All this shows 
that we may be conservative in 
estimating energy storage needs 
for next five years.
During FY 2026, we operationalised 
1.3 GWh of BESS capacity in 
Rajasthan, taking our total 
operational BESS p

ortfolio to 
3.6 GWh7. This marks a significant 
milestone in our storage journey 
and reinforces our position as an 
early mover in utility-scale BESS 
deployment in India. The duck 
curve created due to scaled 
operationalisation of renewable 
capacity in the industry is creating 
a significant arbitrage opportunity 
for BESS operations, as electricity 
prices decline during mid-day 
hours and spike up during the 
evening peak. This enables us to 
procure power from the market 
at lower tariffs during the day 
and sell it at higher prices during 
peak non-solar hours through our 
BESS operations.
We have also made significant 
progress in securing grid 
connectivity for our storage 
portfolio. We have secured over 
10 GWh of BESS connectivity, with 
a further 11 GWh of connectivity 
applications submitted under 
the CERC right-of-first-refusal 
(ROFR) framework currently under 
approval.7 Our development 
strategy is focused on leveraging 
available connectivity to 
commission battery-linked, 
night-time capacity ahead of the 
corresponding commissioning 
of FDRE projects as per 
GNA timelines.
This approach enables us to 
phase capital deployment 
more efficiently, front-loading 
investments that can be 
commissioned and generate 
revenue earlier, while aligning 
subsequent solar investments 
with grid readiness. It also 
provides greater flexibility in 
managing potential connectivity 
delays and reduces the impact 
of such delays on overall project 
timelines and cash generation.
Storage-based power has 
consequently become a 
significant component of our 
portfolio, reflecting our transition 
beyond a pure-play solar model. 
The increasing integration of 
BESS strengthens our ability to 
provide reliable and dispatchable 
renewable power, while 
enhancing portfolio flexibility, 
optimising capital deployment 
and positioning us to address 
the evolving requirements of 
India’s power grid.

is overcoming the intermittency of solar and wind power. Battery Energy Storage 
Systems (BESS) are redefining this paradigm by enabling clean energy to be stored, 
shifted and delivered when demand is highest, transforming renewable power into 
firm, dispatchable and round-the-clock energy solutions.

journey by cumulatively operationalising 3.6 GWh1

in Rajasthan as of 31st July 2026, positioning us 
among the early movers in India to achieve storage 
deployment at this scale.
We have proactively adapted our development 
strategy to address evolving grid connectivity 
requirements. We have secured night-time 
connectivity under CERC’s right-of-first-refusal 
framework and have prioritised the development of 
assets that can be commissioned ahead of full GNA 
connectivity. We have secured BESS connectivity of

applications submitted under the RoFR framework 
currently under approval.2

sting solar plants, we are

new solar deployment with the availability of full 
GNA timelines.

Market Context
India has crossed 500 GW of installed power generation capacity, with 
renewable energy accounting for approximately 275 GW (52%) of the total 
installed capacity as of March 2026. Renewable sources contributed around 
25% of total electricity generation during FY 2026, supported by continued 
additions in solar and wind capacity. Backed by the Government's target 
of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, the sector is witnessing 
sustained investment across renewable generation, storage and 
transmission infrastructure.
The power market is simultaneously witnessing widening intraday tariff 
differentials. While abundant daytime renewable generation can reduce 
tariffs to as low as INR 0.05 per unit, peak and night-time demand can 
command tariffs of up to INR 10 per unit, significantly strengthening the 
commercial case for storage-backed renewable solutions. At the same 
time, transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity remain critical 
enablers, with limited connectivity availability expected until FY 2028–FY 2029, 
influencing project execution timelines and pipeline conversion.

storage deployment and accelerating industry adoption.

Market Context
India's renewable energy ambitions are entering an execution-intensive 
phase. As project sizes increase and the industry transitions towards 
integrated Solar, Wind, Hybrid, FDRE and Battery Energy Storage 
System (BESS) projects, developers require significantly higher capital 
deployment, execution capabilities and supply chain coordination. 
According to CRISIL Intelligence, India's power sector is expected to 
attract INR 37–42 trillion of investments during FY 2027-FY 2031, with a 
substantial share directed towards renewable generation, transmission 
and distribution infrastructure. As the sector scales, timely project 
execution, access to long-term financing, grid connectivity and efficient 
capital allocation are becoming key differentiators for developers. In 
parallel, procurement models are evolving from standalone renewable 
projects towards integrated renewable and storage solutions, requiring 
larger upfront investments, longer development cycles and stronger 
balance sheets. Developers with integrated project development, 
EPC and O&M capabilities, diversified funding sources and disciplined 
capital allocation are expected to be better positioned to execute 
complex projects at scale while main

To address grid intermittency and accelerate 
clean energy integration, India’s power sector is 
undergoing a structural transition driven by the 
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and 
implementing agencies like SECI and SJVN. During 
FY 2025–26, bidding activity shifted decisively away 
from standalone solar toward complex multi-
technology tenders, including Wind-Solar Hybrid 
(WSH), Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy 
(FDRE), and Round-the-Clock (RTC) configurations 
backed by Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). 
While conventional solar and wind offer variable 
outputs, hybrid systems leverage complementary 
diurnal cycles to achieve Capacity Utilisation 
Factors (CUFs). FDRE and RTC projects advance this 
by combining storage with calculated capacity 
overbuild, providing power system reliability 
comparable to conventional thermal plants.
Consequently, FDRE tenders emerged as a 
cost-effective, rapidly deployable alternative to 
new coal-fired assets. Conventional thermal power 
plants demand substantial capital investments, 
carry volatile fuel risks, face execution delays, and 
yield long-term tariffs averaging INR 4–INR 5/kWh.31 
In contrast, FDRE projects feature accelerated 
execution windows and fixed long-term pricing, 
offering a stable and scalable framework to meet 
India’s

Growth Drivers
Rising Power Demand
India’s electricity consumption rose 11.5% y-o-y to 
164.98 billion units (BU) in May 2026, while peak power 
demand touched a record 270.82 GW amid rising 
temperatures and increased energy requirements 
across the country.34 This sustained upswing is 
driven by factors such as accelerated structural 
economic development, seasonal fluctuations, and 
a pronounced rise in the country’s average daily 
temperatures over the past decade.
India’s power demand is tightly linked to its 
macroeconomic performance, with rapid GDP growth, 
driving baseline energy needs. As the fastest-growing 
major economy globally, demand is being boosted by 
initiatives such as nationwide railway electrification, 
the expansion of regional metro networks, increasing 
electric vehicle adoption, and heightened activity 
in the manufacturing and infrastructure sectors. 
Over the next five years, electricity consumption is 
projected to grow at a CAGR of 5.5–6%, supported by 
heavy capital investment in transmission grids and 
distribution systems. Government-led distribution 
reforms are expected to enhance power supply 
quality, further stimulating demand. Consequently, 
peak electricity demand is anticipated to rise rapidly, 
with projections from the Ministry of Power targeting 
300 GW as early as next year, driven by ongoing 
urbanisation, extreme climate variations, and  
large-scale manufacturing expansion.35

Management Discussion and Analysis
Declining Tariffs and Solar Module Prices
Driven by technological advancements, 
manufacturing scale and global oversupply, solar 
module prices have declined sharply from around 
USD 1.8/W in 2010 to nearly USD 0.1/W, improving the 
economics of utility-scale solar projects. At the same 
time, India’s solar market is increasingly shaped by 
domestic-content requirements. ALMM List-I covers 
solar PV modules, while ALMM List-II covers solar PV 
cells; the Government has also initiated measures 
relating to approved manufacturers for upstream 
components such as wafers and ingots.36 For ACME 
Solar, only three projects currently have ALMM List-II 
applicability — the SECI FDRE projects with tariffs 
of INR 6/kWh, the SJVN FDRE projects with tariffs of 
INR 7/kWh, and the REMCL RTC bids. The remaining 
projects are exempt from ALMM List-II requirements, 
as their bids were submitted prior to 31st August 2025.
In parallel, the phased withdrawal of Inter-State 
Transmission System (ISTS) charge waivers is 
influencing the economics of inter-state renewable 
power. Under the current framework, the waiver for 
eligible solar projects commissioned after June 2025 
reduces progressively, with applicable ISTS charges 
increasing from 25% in FY 2026 to 50% in FY 2027, 
75% in FY 2028 and 100% thereafter. The Government 
has also clarified that eligible projects delayed 
due to transmission-system unavailability can 
retain the applicable graded waiver, subject to 
specified conditions.
The extension of the waiver mechanism for eligible 
projects facing transmission delays provides 
greater clarity to DISCOMs and can help protect the 
economics of contracted projects. For ACME Solar, 
this creates an opportunity for eligible off-takers 
to avail the applicable ISTS waiver where General 
Network Access (GNA) or transmission infrastructure 
is del

ayed, supporting the competitiveness of the 
Company’s contracted projects.
These policy dynamics, alongside declining 
technology costs, continue to shape tariff 
competitiveness and procurement decisions 
in India’s renewable energy market. In major 
government auctions during FY 2026, including those 
conducted by GUVNL, discovered tariffs reached INR 
2.34/kWh, with project-specific factors such as grid 
connectivity and state regulations resulting in tariffs 
of up to INR 3.05/kWh.37
Fiscal and Policy Incentives
The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) 
has maintained its structured, annual bidding 
trajectory of 50 GW of renewable energy capacity 
(including at least 10 GW of wind) rolling through to 
FY 2027–28. This framework is specifically designed to 
meet the nation’s ambitious 500 GW non-fossil 
fuel capacity target by 2030.38 Furthermore, 
the successful operational integration of core 
central-level allocations, such as the Jawaharlal 
Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM) pathways, 
alongside the continuous infrastructure expansion of 
dedicated ultra-mega solar parks, underscores the 
government’s sustained focus on solar power as the 
primary driver of its national energy transition.
Domestic supply chain resilience has been 
significantly strengthened by the Production 
Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. Under the National 
Programme on High Efficiency Solar PV Modules, a 
dedicated fiscal allocation of INR 240,000 million 
has driven massive gigawatt-scale capacity setup 
across the upstream manufacturing value chain.39 
By the close of FY 2026, India’s cumulative domestic 
solar module manufacturing capacity expanded 
rapidly to approximately 172 GW. Concurrently, the 
phased deployment of Intra-state and Inter-state 
Green Energy Corridors has scaled up to handle 
the transmission of this record high-volume clean 
generation.40

Robust regulatory and grid infrastructure 
interventions have also accelerated the Wind-
Solar Hybrid and energy storage segments. 
Recognising that wind and solar resources exhibit 
highly complementary diurnal and seasonal 
generation patterns, the government has leveraged 
these synergies to foster a more reliable, grid-
stable electricity supply. When integrated with 
battery storage (BESS) or Pumped Storage Projects 
(PSPs), these configurations facilitate near 24x7 
Round-the-Clock (RTC) clean power delivery, 
successfully mitigating the core challenges of 
renewable intermittency.
Ultimately, a cohesive suite of policy levers has 
established a highly conducive commercial 
environment for project developers. This ecosystem 
is sustained by progressively rising Renewable 
Purchase Obligation (RPO) pathways, Viability Gap 
Funding (VGF) windows for storage integration, 
extended Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) grid 
charge waivers, and the security of structured, state-
backed utility solar park plug-and-play frameworks.
Focus on Energy Storage Systems (ESS) and 
Complex Solutions
Energy storage technologies enhance grid stability 
by storing excess energy when demand is low and 
releasing it during peak times. Lithium-based battery 
solutions are progressing quickly, with constant 
structural breakthroughs in materials, cell designs, 
manufacturing, and alternative chemistries shaping 
their utility.
Between 2020 and 2026, the cost of lithium-ion 
batteries dropped sharply, driven by technological 
improvements, lower prices of key raw materials like 
lithium, cobalt, and nickel, and a rapid expansion 
in global manufacturing capacity. Global cell costs 
have declined for Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) 
architectures and Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) 
options. This decline has significantly increased the 
commercial viability and attractiveness of Battery 
Energy Storage Systems (BE

SS) in power projects, 
triggering high industry participation in recent 
storage auctions. Beyond 2030, solid-state batteries 
are expected to achieve commercial availability, 
promising significant performance leaps.
The Government is actively promoting domestic 
battery manufacturing, targeting a battery 
production capacity of 200 GWh by 2030.41 This 
policy directly aligns with the strategic requirements 
mapped by the International Energy Agency (IEA) 
in its Critical Minerals Data Explorer, which provides 
global demand projections for 37 critical minerals 
needed for clean energy transitions across the 
three main IEA scenarios and 11 technology-specific 
cases.42
Beyond supply-side incentives, the sector is being 
supported by regulatory measures that are improving 
the viability and flexibility of BESS deployment. 
CTU has begun processing BESS connectivity 
applications under the Right of First Refusal (RoFR) 
framework, while allowing BESS projects to utilise 
available ISTS grid margins for charging, subject to 
applicable conditions and discharge it during non-
solar hours using the same existing transmission 
infrastructure which increases the overall utilisation 
of transmission lines. For projects opting to install 
commensurate renewable generation, the current 
framework provides up to 36 months from the 
applicable connectivity start point to commission 
the associated renewable generation for charging 
the BESS, supporting a phased approach to 
storage deployment.
The regulatory framework is also evolving to provide 
greater certainty around projects affected by 
transmission delays. CERC has proposed measures 
under its 2026 connectivity and GNA framework to 
provide additional flexibility around connectivity 
and commissioning timelines, while compensation 
mechanisms apply in specified cases. CERC has 
given regulatory certainty to those projects which 
are delayed with respect to connectivity timelines 
and allowed a period of up to 12 month

s beyond 
the GNA effectiveness date or start date with 
compensation charges. Separately, the Ministry of 
Power has provided for extension of applicable ISTS 
waiver benefits where projects are delayed due to 
transmission connectivity, subject to the relevant 
commissioning slabs and conditions.
Taking cognisance of the fact that BESS projects 
can commission much earlier as compared to 
its associated RE for charging, MNRE and MoP has 
also clarified that wherever BESS component is 
commissioned prior to SCOD but its RE is under-
construction, the developers can utilise such BESS 
for merchant sale of power using conventional grid 
power without requiring consent or NOC from REIA/
buying entity. Thus, it creates opportunity for those 
projects where grid substation is either operational 
or bay is charged for BESS component as BESS 
can be deployed in merchant mode ahead of the 
associated renewable capacity, enabling storage 
assets to generate cash flows while grid connectivity 
for the broader project is being established. 
Concurrently, interest has surged in standalone ESS 
projects and integrated configurations such as Firm 
and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) and 
Round-the-Clock (RTC) projects.

Management Discussion and Analysis
FDRE projects deliver reliable, on-demand power 
by integrating variable solar and wind with energy 
storage systems. This configuration ensures a 
consistent supply of electricity, even when natural 
conditions are unfavourable, enhancing grid stability 
and reducing reliance on fossil fuels. RTC projects 
take this further by guaranteeing 24/7 power 
availability through a mix of renewable sources 
and storage, often complemented by flexible 
generation assets. These models are pivotal in India’s 
transition to a low-carbon energy system, offering 
utilities and indust

ries dependable green power at 
competitive tariffs.
In recent large-scale allocations, out of a total 77 
GW of competitive bids, solar projects accounted 
for roughly 60 GW. and wind projects made up 
remaining 17 GW.43
Availability of Low-cost Financing
Low-cost financing is crucial for India to deploy 
utility-scale renewable energy and hit its 500 GW 
non-fossil fuel capacity target by 2030. To drive this, 
the government granted the clean energy sector 
Priority Sector Lending (PSL) status. Dedicated public 
financial institutions, specifically REC, PFC, IREDA, 
SBI and NaBFID, provide easy access to large-scale 
capital at competitive interest rates. Backed by its 
Navratna status, IREDA’s loan book expanded 22% 
to cross a record INR 93,075 crores by the close of 
FY 2026, proving a massive scaling up of active green 
infrastructure credit.44 
International partnerships, leveraged during 
India’s G20 Presidency and expanding through 
contemporary BRICS and global clean energy 
frameworks, increasingly focus on blended finance 
models and multilateral funding. These instruments 
are designed to de-risk capital injections into 
emerging technologies like offshore wind, green 
hydrogen, and battery storage.
Technological Advancements
The solar power sector continues to achieve 
significant efficiency gains driven by rapid 
technological advancements across module design 
and cell architecture. In particular, the industry-
wide adoption of bifacial module designs, utilising 
dual-pane glass construction or reflective back 
sheets, allows modules to capture light from both 
sides, optimising power generation and maximising 
overall energy yield while minimising land and 
resource consumption.
Simultaneously, global cell manufacturing is 
transitioning rapidly toward Tunnel Oxide Passivated 
Contact (TOPCon) technology.45 By delivering higher 
conversion efficiencies and lower temperature 
degradation compared to traditional P-type cells, 
TOPCon enables superior

energy capture. Furthermore, 
because TOPCon manufacturing processes can be 
integrated into legacy Passivated Emitter and Rear 
Cell (PERC) production lines with minimal capital 
equipment upgrades, it has emerged as the prevailing 
standard for utility-scale solar expansion.46
As the country moves towards self-reliance in solar 
manufacturing, India’s cumulative domestic solar 
module manufacturing capacity expanded rapidly 
to approximately 172 GW by the close of FY 2026.47 
Reflecting this growth, solar cell and module imports 
dropped by 2.8% y-o-y during the Q1 cycle.48 The 
industry is systematically transitioning from older 
p-type architectures to high-efficiency n-type solar 
cell technologies (including TOPCon, Heterojunction 
Technology (HJT), and back contact designs), 
which deliver higher cell efficiency and overall cost 
reductions despite material intensity challenges 
regarding critical mineral inputs.
Favourable Conditions for Wind capacity
India’s wind energy sector continued to expand in 
FY 2026, with cumulative installed capacity crossing 
56 GW and approximately 6.05 GW added during the 
year. Policy support, including the Wind Renewable 
Consumption Obligation and growing adoption of 
wind-solar hybrid projects, continues to support the 
sector’s development. For ACME Solar, wind remains 
a complementary technology within its diversified 
renewable energy portfolio, supporting hybrid and 
firm, dispatchable renewable energy solutions 
alongside solar and BESS.

Management Discussion and Analysis
Environment
As a lead

ing renewable energy company, 
sustainability considerations are integrated into our 
operations and project-development processes. 
We maintain defined environmental targets and 
performance indicators, including achieving water 
neutrality and zero waste to landfill across operating 
sites, and eliminating specified single-use plastics 
from operations across operating sites, by 2030.
Our operating framework combines in-house EPC 
and O&M capabilities with digital monitoring and 
resource-efficient technologies to support reliable 
plant performance. These include waterless robotic 
module-cleaning systems at applicable solar 
projects, round-the-clock SCADA-based monitoring, 
reactive power management and high-efficiency 
bifacial TOPCon modules.
We also aim to complete climate-risk screening 
across 100% of operating sites and under-
construction projects by FY 2029, followed by 
detailed climate-resilience assessments and 
adaptation planning for sites and projects 
identified as materially exposed. Our broader 
environmental initiatives include responsible waste 
management, circular economy practices and 
biodiversity conservation.

Social
At ACME Solar, we invest in professional development 
and continuous learning to empower personnel, drive 
growth, and embed future-ready capabilities across 
the business. Concurrently, we enforce rigorous policies, 
including our updated Health, Safety, and Environment 
(HSE) framework and Human Resources guidelines, to 
maintain a respectful, inclusive, and highly productive 
workplace. Beyond these internal structures, we create 
measurable social impact through targeted Corporate 
Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives, including 
extensive afforestation and community development 
programmes that foster environmental restoration and 
long-term community engagement.
Read more on page no. 56.
Governance
At ACME Solar, we champion an ethical corporate 
culture through explicit policy frameworks,

ensuring 
proactive Board-level oversight and absolute 
compliance with evolving legal and statutory 
mandates. Our structure integrates stringent risk 
management, comprehensive information security 
protocols, and an uncompromised Code of Conduct, 
all reinforced by routine employee training and 
independent audits. We steadily adapt to legislative 
updates and enforce a zero-tolerance approach 
toward any regulatory non-compliance.

Risk management is a continuous endeavour 
at ACME Solar. We have established a robust risk

35.	 DISCLOSURE UNDER EMPLOYEES STOCK 
OPTION PLANS AND SCHEMES
	
The Company had adopted the ACME Employee 
Stock Option Plan 2024 
(“ESOP Scheme”) 
pursuant to approval from the shareholders in 
their meetings held on 27th June 2024, 08th October 
2024, 17th October 2024 and 21st February 2025, 
with a view to reward employee performance 
and dedication towards the Company; retain, 
attract and motivate employees and encourage 
employees to align performance with the

Company’s objectives and goals. Further, the 
renewable industry is witnessing high growth 
resulting in a demand-supply gap for talent, 
necessitating long-term incentive programs 
such as the ESOP Scheme.
	
During the period from the end of the financial 
year and till the date of this report, the ESOP 
Scheme has been reviewed to align it with the 
governance and regulatory framework applicable 
to listed companies. As part of this review, certain 
provisions primarily relevant to the period when 
the Company was an unlisted entity were 
identified for deletion or modification. Accordingly, 
the Board of Directors, at its meeting held on 
07th May 2026, based on the recommendation of 
the Nomination and Remuneration Committee 
approved certain amendments to the ESOP 
Scheme, to inter alia: (a) delete provisions that 
were applicable only to the pre-listing phase 
of the Company; (b)  remove references and 
procedural provisions which are no longer 
relevant after listing; and (c) incorporate certain 
administrative clarifications to facilitate efficient 
implementation and administration of the ESOP 
Scheme in a listed company environment.
	
Further, in order to align the interests of 
employees with those of the Company and its 
subsidiary(ies) and/or holding company(ies), and 
to attract, retain and incentivize talent across the 
group and to create a sense of ownership and 
participation amongst them, the benefits of the 
ESOP Scheme were proposed to be extended to 
eligible employees of the subsidiary(ies) and/or 
holding company(ies) of the Company by way of 
a separate shareholders’ resolution.
	
Subsequently, the members of the Company 
approved (a) the above-mentioned amendments 
to the ESOP Scheme and (b) grant of options to 
the eligible employees of the subsidiary(ies) 
and/or holding company(ies) of the Company 
under the ESOP Scheme, through postal ballot on 
12th June 2026.
	
During the FY 2026, Company has granted 3,911,414 
stock options unde

r the ESOP Scheme. A detailed 
report with respect to options exercised, vested, 
lapsed, exercise price, vesting period is annexed 
as Annexure E to this report. Further, the ESOP 
Scheme is in compliance with SEBI (Share Based 
Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 
2021 (“SEBI SBEB Regulations”). The Company 
formed an irrevocable trust under the name 
and style of “ACME Employees Welfare Trust” 
for the purpose of administration of the ESOP 
Scheme. The ESOP Scheme is implemented and 
administered through a trust route for extending 
the benefits to the eligible employees.
	
The certificate from the Secretarial Auditor of 
the Company, that the ESOP Scheme has been 
implemented in accordance with the SEBI SBEB 
Regulations along with the resolutions passed by 
the Members, would be available for electronic 
inspection by the Members at the ensuing 
11th AGM.
	
Further, the details specified under Regulation 14 
of the SEBI SBEB Regulations, are available on the 
Company’s website at

Does the entity have any project related to reducing Green House Gas emission? If Yes, then provide 
details.
	
Yes. ACME Solar’s core business is a greenhouse-gas-reduction enterprise. Our operational solar, wind 
and hybrid capacity generates clean electricity that replaces fossil-fuel-based generation and avoids 
substantial CO2-equivalent emissions each year.
	
During FY 2025-26, ACME Solar enabled the avoidance of approximately 4.53 million tCO2e (4,530,947.49 
tonnes CO2 equivalent) emissions through the generation of renewable electricity. Emissions avoided 
were calculated by multiplying the total renewable energy gene

rated (MWh) by the Central Electricity 
Authority (CEA) Grid Emission Factor of 0.71 tCO2/MWh (CEA Baseline Database, 2025). This reflects ACME 
Solar’s contribution to decarbonizing India’s power sector and supporting the country’s transition towards 
a low-carbon energy future.
	
In addition, the Company reduces the emission-intensity of its own operations through: (i) robotic and water-
efficient module-cleaning systems that reduce diesel and water use; (ii) development of firm and dispatchable 
renewable (hybrid/FDRE) projects that aid grid decarbonisation; (iii) progressive replacement of diesel gensets 
with solar/battery back-up at sites; and (iv) energy-efficiency measures across offices and O&M facilities. 
These initiatives support India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and the Company’s ESG commitments.

Report on Corporate Governance
At ACME Solar Holdings Limited (“Company”), corporate 
governance is an integral part of the way we conduct 
our business. It is founded on the principles of integrity, 
transparency, accountability and fairness, and serves 
as the foundation for responsible decision-making 
and sustainable value creation. We believe that strong 
governance is not defined solely by compliance with 
laws and regulations, but by consistently acting 
in the best interests of our shareholders and all 
other

stakeholders.
Our governance framework has been developed to 
support the Company’s long-term strategy while 
ensuring effective oversight, prudent risk management 
and ethical business conduct. Clearly defined roles, 
robust internal controls and structured decision-
making processes enable us to operate responsibly 
and respond effectively to an evolving business and 
regulatory environment.
The Board of Directors provides strategic leadership and 
oversees the Company’s performance, governance 
practices and risk management framework. It is 
supported by various Board Committees, each 
entrusted with specific responsibilities relating to audit, 
risk management, nomination and remuneration, 
stakeholder relationships and corporate social 
responsibility & sustainability. Together, the Board and 
its Committees promote informed decision-making, 
independent oversight and balanced governance 
across the organisation.
We recognise that effective governance extends 
beyond financial oversight. Accordingly, the Company 
has established systems for internal controls, cyber 
security, data protection and information security. 
These systems are periodically reviewed and 
strengthened through independent assessments and 
continuous monitoring to address emerging risks and 
changing regulatory expectations.
The Company remains committed to maintaining 
transparent and timely communication with investors, 
regulators and other stakeholders. We endeavour 
to provide accurate, complete and meaningful 
disclosures relating to our financial performance, 
material developments, related party transactions 
and other matters that may influence stakeholder 
decisions. Our disclosure practices are aligned with the 
requirements of the Securities and Exchange Board of 
India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI Listing Regulations”), 
Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”) and other applicable laws 
and regulations.
Company’s Philosophy on Corporate 
Gov

ernance
The Company’s approach to corporate governance 
is guided by the belief that responsible business 
practices are essential for sustainable growth. Our 
governance philosophy is built upon the values of 
integrity, transparency, fairness, accountability and 
professionalism. These values shape our decisions, 
strengthen stakeholder confidence and support the 
creation of long-term value.
Compliance with applicable laws, regulations and 
governance standards is a fundamental responsibility. 
At the same time, we endeavour to foster a culture 
where ethical conduct, sound judgement and 
responsible decision-making become an integral 
part of everyday business practices rather than 
merely fulfilling statutory obligations.
To reinforce this commitment, the Company has 
adopted comprehensive policies and governance 
mechanisms covering areas such as prevention 
of 
insider 
trading, 
related 
party 
transactions, 
whistleblower protection, enterprise risk management, 
information security and regulatory compliance. 
These frameworks encourage transparency, promote 
accountability and support a culture of integrity 
across all levels of the organisation.
We believe that corporate governance is most effective 
when it is embedded in the organisational culture. Every 
employee, member of management and Director shares 
the responsibility of upholding the Company’s values and 
maintaining the trust placed in us by our stakeholders.

Performance evaluation
	
The 
Board 
recognises 
that 
a 
meaningful 
evaluation process supports its effectiveness, 
strengthens 
accountability 
and 
promotes 
continuous 
improvement 
in 
governance. 
Accordingly, based on the recommendation of 
the Nomination and Remuneration Committee, 
the Board adopted a structured framework for 
evaluating the performance of the Board as 
a whole, its Committees, the Chairperson and 
individual Directors.
	
The evaluation for FY2026 was undertaken 
through structured questionnaires tailored to 
the responsibilities of the Board, its Committees, 
the Chairperson and individual Directors. The 
assessment considered, among other matters, 
the quality

and effectiveness of deliberations, 
fulfilment 
of 
responsibilities, 
Board 
and 
Committee composition, quality and timeliness 
of 
information, 
participation 
in 
meetings, 
oversight of strategy and risk, and the overall 
contribution to the Company’s governance and 
decision-making.
	
The evaluation of the Independent Directors was 
undertaken by the entire Board, excluding the 
Director being evaluated, in accordance with 
Regulation 17(10) of the SEBI Listing Regulations. The 
criteria included preparedness and participation 
in meetings, knowledge of the Company’s 
business and operating environment, exercise of 
independent judgement, contribution to strategy, 
governance and risk oversight, constructive 
engagement with management, safeguarding 
stakeholder 
interests, 
and 
adherence 
to 
applicable duties, the Code of Conduct and 
conflict-of-interest requirements. The evaluation 
framework was informed by the principles set out 
in SEBI’s Guidance Note on Board Evaluation..

risk and hedging activities:

Company 
does

derivative financial instruments are initially 
recognised at fair value on the date on which 
a derivative contract is entered into and are 
subsequently re-measured at fair value. 
Derivatives are carried as financial assets 
when the fair value is positive and as financial 
liabilities when the fair value is negative. The 
Company is exposed to foreign exchange risk 
on account of its payables in foreign currency.

Impairment assessment of carrying values of investments in 
and loans given to subsidiaries
Refer note 2.1(m) and 2.1(g) in material accounting policy 
information and note 6 and 15 in notes forming part of 
standalone financial statements in relation to investments in 
and loans to subsidiaries.
As at 31st March 2026, the Company has investments in and 
loans given to subsidiaries aggregating to INR 75,623.99 million, 
which constitutes 58.43% of the total assets of the Company.
At each period end, the management reviews whether any 
impairment indicators exist in the carrying value of investments, 
in accordance with the requirements of Ind AS 36, “Impairment 
of Assets” (‘Ind AS 36’), and whether there is any significant 
increase in credit risk in loans receivables in accordance with 
the requirements of Ind AS 109, “Financial instruments” (‘Ind AS 
109’). In respect of investments and loans where impairment 
indicators are identified or significant increase in credit risk is 
noted, the management performs a detailed impairment test 
by determining the recoverable value of such balances.
As at 31st March 2026, the carrying value of investment in 14 
subsidiaries was higher than their net worth, which has been 
identified as an impairment indicator by the mana

gement in 
accordance with Ind AS 36.
The management has estimated the recoverable amount of its 
investment in such subsidiaries using the ‘Discounted Cash Flow 
valuation model’. The future cash flows were projected based 
on the Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) entered with the 
customers for a long term and the present value of such cash 
flows were derived using a discount rate.
As per such assessment done by the management, no 
further adjustments are required to the carrying value of the 
investments in and loans given to such subsidiaries as at 
31st March 2026.
Considering the significance of aforesaid balances to the overall 
financial statements, the large number of entities and degree of 
judgement involved in assumptions used for the computation 
of the recoverable amount, we have considered impairment 
assessment of carrying value of investments in and loans given 
to subsidiaries as a key audit matter for the current year audit.
Our audit procedures in relation to impairment assessment 
of the carrying values of investments in and loans given to 
subsidiaries included, but were not limited to the following:
•	 Obtained an understanding of the management’s process 
for identification of impairment indicators for investments 
and significant increase in credit risk of loans, and evaluated 
the design and tested the operating effectiveness of key 
internal financial controls relating to such process;
•	 Evaluated the Company’s accounting policies with 
respect to impairment assessment and assessed its 
compliance with the requirements of Ind AS 36 and 
Ind AS 109;
•	 Obtained the management’s assessment on impairment 
indicators around the recoverability of investment in and 
loans given to subsidiaries and tested the mathematical 
accuracy of the underlying calculations and traced such 
information to source financial information relating to 
subsidiary companies;
•	 For cases where impairment indicators presents, obtained 
the impairment assessment wor

king from the management 
and tested the arithmetical accuracy of valuation model 
and traced the future cash flow projections used for 
determining recoverable amount with the approved 
business plans and signed PPAs entered with the customers;
•	 Performed sensitivity analysis of the key assumptions, 
including the discount rate applied in determining the 
recoverable value to evaluate the possible variation on the 
current recoverable amount to ascertain the sufficiency of 
headroom available;
•	 Reviewed the regularity of repayment of principal and 
payments of interest as per terms of the agreement relating 
to loans given to the subsidiary companies; and
•	 Evaluated the appropriateness and adequacy of disclosures 
given in the standalone financial statements in accordance 
with applicable accounting standards.

1.	
In conjunction with our audit of the standalone 
financial statements of ACME Solar Holdings 
Limited (formerly known as ACME Solar Holdings 
Private Limited) (‘the Company’) as at and f

or 
the year ended 31st March 2026, we have audited 
the internal financial controls with reference 
to financial statements of the Company as at

Responsibilities of Management and Those 
Charged with Governance for Internal 
Financial Controls
2.	
The Company’s Board of Directors is responsible 
for 
establishing 
and 
maintaining 
internal 
financial controls based on the internal controls 
with reference to the financial statements criteria 
established by the Company considering the 
essential component of internal control stated 
in Guidance note on Audit of Internal Financial 
Controls over Financial Reporting issued by 
the Institute of Chartered Accountant of India. 
These 
responsibilities 
include 
the 
design, 
implementation and maintenance of adequate 
internal financial controls that were operating 
effectively for ensuring the orderly and efficient 
conduct of the Company’s business, including 
adherence to the Company’s policies, the 
safeguarding of its assets, the prevention and 
detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy 
and completeness of the accounting records, 
and the timely preparation of reliable financial 
information, as required under the Act.
Auditor’s Responsibility for the Audit of the 
Internal Financial Controls with Reference to 
Financial Statements
3.	
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on 
the Company’s internal financial controls with 
reference to financial statements based on our 
audit. We conducted our audit in accordance 
with the Standards on Auditing issued by the 
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (‘ICAI’) 
prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the 
extent applicable to an audit of internal financial 
controls with reference to financial statements, 
and the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal 
Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting 
(‘the Guidance Note’) issued by the ICAI. Those 
Standards and the Guidance Note require that 
we comply with ethical requirements and plan

and perform the audit to obtain reasonable 
assurance about whether adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements were established and maintained 
and if such controls operated effectively in all 
material respects.
4.	
Our audit involves performing procedures to 
obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of 
the internal financial controls with reference 
to financial statements and their operating 
effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial 
controls with reference to financial statements 
includes obtaining an understanding of such 
internal financial controls, assessing the risk 
that a material weakness exists, and testing 
and evaluating the design and operating 
effectiveness of internal control based on the 
assessed risk. The procedures selected depend 
on the auditor’s judgement, including the 
assessment of the risks of material misstatement 
of the financial statements, whether due to fraud 
or error.
5.	
We believe that the audit evidence we have 
obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide 
a basis for our audit opinion on the Company’s 
internal financial controls with reference to 
financial statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with 
Reference to Financial Statements
6.	
A company’s internal financial controls with 
reference to financial statements is a process 
designed to provide reasonable assurance 
regarding the reliability of financial reporting 
and the preparation of financial statements for 
external purposes in accordance with generally 
accepted accounting principles. A company’s 
internal financial controls with reference to 
financial statements include those policies and 
procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of 
records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and

the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable 
assurance that transactions are recorded as

generally 
accepted accounting principles, and that receipts 
and expenditures of the company are being 
made only in accordance with authorisations 
of management and directors of the company; 
and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding 
prevention or timely detection of unauthorised 
acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s 
assets that could have a material effect on the 
financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial 
Controls with Reference to Financial 
Statements
7.	
Because of the inherent limitations of internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements, including the possibility of collusion 
or improper management override of controls, 
material misstatements due to error or fraud 
may occur and not be detected. Also, projections 
of any evaluation of the internal financial controls 
with reference to financial statements to future 
periods are subject to the risk that the internal 
financial controls with reference to financial 
statements may become inadequate because 
of changes in conditions, or that the degree of 
compliance with the policies or procedures 
may deteriorate.
Opinion

In our opinion, the Company has, in all material 
respects, adequate internal financial controls 
with reference to financial statements and 
such controls were operating effectively as at 
31st March 2026, based on the internal controls 
with reference to financial statements criteria 
established by the Company considering the
